PROVISION RESPECTING USE ON CEREMONIAL OCCASIONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-153 entitled "An act respecting the use of the Canadian flag on ceremonial occasions."

subtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING USE ON CEREMONIAL OCCASIONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING USE ON CEREMONIAL OCCASIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Union Jack is usually hoisted in the presence of Her Majesty the Queen of Canada or her representative on public occasions or ceremonies. Now, Her Majesty the Queen of Canada is also chief of the Canadian state and acts as such in our country; therefore, it seems that in the presence of the chief of the Canadian state, the Canadian flag can be hoisted as well as the flag usually hoisted according to the established custom.
This is the object of the present bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-SPEECH AT UN BY EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER-VISIT TO CANADA BY ALLEGED STUDENTS
speechtext:
I have a question to address to the Prime Minister. It is in reference to the interesting address made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the United Nations general assembly in which he urged cessation of the bombing of North Viet Nam and declared also-I quote-that "there is no hope for progress toward a peaceful settlement in appeals or proposals which place the total burden on one side only."
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government is planning to follow up this statement by negotiations or discussions with other parties involved designed to
bring about an improvement in this most dangerous situation. In particular I should like to know whether any new overtures are being planned to the authorities at Hanoi or their allies to end the flow of troops and war materials from North Viet Nam to South Viet Nam should the bombing cease.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-SPEECH AT UN BY EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER-VISIT TO CANADA BY ALLEGED STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is at the moment on his way back to Ottawa. I had hoped that he would be in his seat to deal with this particular matter, but he will not be here until tomorrow morning now.
I know discussions have been going on with other governments as to what steps can be taken to follow up the various proposals which have been made in connection with this conflict. There are no special steps I know of that are being taken, certainly not by us, with Hanoi at the moment, but perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs can add to my reply tomorrow. He has been in touch with a good many delegations at the United Nations and may be able to add to what I have said.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a related question for the Prime Minister. I wish to ask whether the Prime Minister can tell us what is the purpose of the visit to Canada by members of the Vietnamese liberation front, which is a communist organization currently engaged in active hostilities against United States forces in Viet Nam. On what grounds were visas granted by the Canadian government for what appears to be a propaganda tour, and has the government received any representation with regard to this matter from Washington?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these students, or so-called students, were invited to Canada by a Quebec students' organization. They are travelling on North Vietnamese passports, which are acceptable under certain conditions for admission to Canada. If they had been travelling on documents issued by the so-called liberation front this would not have been acceptable. We do have a relationship with the government of North Viet Nam

September 28, 1967
Inquiries of the Ministry because of our membership on the international commission, and we recognize their passports as they recognize ours. I do not know what is the purpose of their visit, Mr. Speaker, but in the circumstances it did not seem possible or desirable to refuse the recognition of North Vietnamese passports regularly held by these applicants for admission to this country.
Subject to further examination, I think we have received a query from the United States government as to any information we may have about the nature and purpose of this visit. I should like to look into that part of the question.

speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, estimates of the Department of Labour for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1968. We are on vote No. 35 dealing with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

35. To reimburse Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for expenditures on housing research and community planning, for the amounts of loans for sewage treatment projects forgiven to a province, municipality or municipal sewerage corporation, for contributions made for an urban renewal scheme or pursuant to an urban renewal agreement, for losses resulting from the operation of public housing projects, and for net losses resulting from the sale of mortgages from its portfolio, $25,300,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take it that we are to move directly to vote 35 of the Department of Labour estimates. This is the only item which deals with estimates of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I welcome heartily the opportunity to discuss these estimates, not simply because of the housing problems which admittedly exist but rather because it affords me an opportunity to present to hon. members a statement concerning some aspects of the housing picture which some statements that were made in the house yesterday and the day before indicate are unknown to them.
I wish to put it on the record at the outset that we do have a serious housing situation in Canada, one which is likely to continue for some years to come. No country can grow as fast as Canada is growing and have a concentration of population in certain urban areas without having housing problems. But I do want to make it perfectly clear that these problems are largely centred in the metropolitan areas in this country, and the record shows that fact quite conclusively. The record speaks for itself. I also want to say that while we do have problems centred in certain specific areas, regardless of what hon. members may say about the housing situation, the situation in these specific areas is not indicative of the housing situation which prevails in the majority of our cities and towns.
Oh, oh.

I also wish to point out that very little reference has been made to the fact that the housing problems that arise in metropolitan areas such as Toronto, Vancouver and other cities the size of Hamilton and larger arise not so much out of a reduced volume of housing-in fact there has been a very substantial increase in housing-but out of the unprecedented pace of general development and growth in these areas. Much house building has been going on in Canada though not enough to take care of the phenomenal growth that has taken place in Toronto and certain other areas. I also wish to say that notwithstanding the deterrents to house building this year, in 1967 we shall have in excess of 150,000 starts.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
That is 50,000 too few.

If the hon. member is quoting the report of the Economic Council, he has not read it very carefully. It says that
140,000	starts will take care of the new family formations, the other 50,000 being to replace old houses that should disappear.
Are they not necessary?
Of course they are needed, but one must deal with problems like that in accordance with all the circumstances.
Oh, oh.
They must all be taken into consideration.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members may laugh; hon. members may well laugh, but the 150,000 starts represent a very substantial increase over starts in 1966. This year's starts represent an increase of about 15 per cent over those of 1966, and this increase, I might point out, has been largely made possible by the vast infusion of federal funds to support housing, an infusion that has been felt in every province of Canada.
There are those who would deplore our not reaching a much quoted figure which has been referred to of 200,000 housing starts. But the 200,000 housing starts are forecast for 1970.
Is it not 190,000?
It is not 190,000, with all due respect. The figure is 200,000 for 1970.

But the Economic Council says that we need 190,000-
September 28, 1967
The hon. member can make his speech later. He may then quote from the report.
Oh, oh.

A little closer examination of that report will reveal that this target that I have referred to is four to five years off.
But hon. members must keep in mind that in our society, which is based on freedom of private action, housing, like any other commodity, is subject to economic laws. Temporary setbacks are bound to be endured periodically in the competition which supports private enterprise. But the vital concern is that our long-range objective of 200,000 starts per annum in the early 1970's be attained in the allotted period.
Did the minister say 1870? His speech sounds like a nineteenth century speech.

One would think that the figures which have been quoted are those of the Economic Council; in fact, many of these figures are supplied by Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, and their forecasts are available to everyone.
If we fail to reach the target of 750,000 starts, including the 200,000 replacements over the next few years, certainly, we shall be in a difficult position. I can only say that the government has no intention of letting that happen, and our record will prove just that.
The government has quite a record.

At the beginning of this year we were optimistic that there would be some slackening in the financial and other pressures which plagued housing during 1966. Nevertheless, hon. members, I submit, must acknowledge that in the years 1964, 1965 and 1966 we had record housing completions in this country. We had three records. We also had record housing starts in 1964 and 1965.
In the budget presentation of last year the Minister of Finance and other representative spokesmen of the government appealed to municipalities, provincial governments and business generally to level out the program of expansion that was bursting at the seams. This had to be done and it has been done. We are now beginning to catch up, notwithstanding the lag in housing starts last year. To stimulate the swing back to housing, to encourage house building at the level that had gone on during 1964, 1965 and 1966 and 27053-164i
Supply-Labour
which was suspended during the last several months of last year, the government introduced in November last a new formula for the establishment of the maximum interest rate which would be permissible under the National Housing Act. This rate was raised to 7J per cent, with provision that there would be automatic adjustments quarterly in accordance with the yield on long-term Canada bonds.
Shortly after changing the interest rate the government moved to release the chartered banks from their previous restriction of a 6 per cent maximum interest rate under the Bank Act, and authorized their participation both in N.H.A. and conventional forms of mortgage lending.
No one can deny, if one studies the figures objectively and fairly, that these incentives not only seemed to help but in fact helped considerably. Bringing the banks back into the picture augurs well for housing in the long run.
It should be obvious to any independent thinker that some time would have to elapse before the banks could fully participate in the program. They were authorized to participate in May, and progress of late has been encouraging. I am sure that the situation is even more encouraging to banks and other lending institutions as a result of the announcement I made last night.
Realizing that it would take some time for the banks to come into the picture and for the pendulum to swing-
Might I ask the minister a question? Could he outline the extent of bank participation since the changes were made in the Bank Act and since the budget? Is that figure available?

Yes. During the last three or four months the banks have been coming in at a rate of $10 million or so a month. It is increasing gradually. The new interest rate should stimulate lending, and we are encouraged by what is happening. One can hardly expect the banks to put their money into housing when they can put it somewhere else to better advantage. That is one of the reasons for our step of last night.
I might also say that the government, realizing that it would take some time for the measures that we announced last year to permit the banks to really come into the picture, took further steps in January. For the first time in Canadian history a spring speculative

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
loan program was introduced. This unprecedented move, together with the normal supply of mortgage money and the introduction of the banks into the picture, resulted in an immediate and substantial surge in housing activity in the spring of this year.
By March of 1967 loans under N.H.A. were being processed at a rate four times that of 1966. These loans included not only home ownership loans but very substantial ones for multiple dwellings for rental purposes, primarily in Toronto and other large cities.
Unfortunately, the re-entry of the chartered banks at first fell somewhat short of our expectations, though in fairness I must say that the response has been more encouraging during the last few months. The reason for the lag is not surprising.
While life insurance companies, trust and loan companies historically have directed most of their investment funds to mortgages, the chartered banks in Canada have concentrated their investment and still are, in the more attractive market of consumer loans. These are facts.
Housing, like other forms of real estate, is a particularly inviting investment when the economic cycle has slowed down to an appreciable extent. One can readily confirm that.
This is the greatest speech I have ever listened to.

When the economy is in a buoyant state, as it has been for the last three or four years, other fields of enterprise receive the bulk of private support. That support comes not only from the banks but from other private lending institutions.

Mr. Chairman-
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

I have a limited amount of time at my disposal. I will be glad to answer questions at the end of my remarks.
The report of the Economic Council to which I have already referred suggests that action should be taken to protect housing from the effects of this anti-cyclical force to which I have referred. When the economy is in a buoyant state, there is relatively little money for housing; when otherwise, there is more, more money goes into housing. The Economic Council in its report refers to this fact but makes no suggestions as to what might be done to alter the situation. I think this should be and is one of their responsibilities. They make no suggestion as to what might be done.
Oh, oh.
They are not running the country. You are.

They are I believe, there to make constructive suggestions occasionally, at least. They are a council set up to advise. Not only do they fail to offer suggestions to correct this situation, but there is nothing new in the statement to which I have referred. Any student of economics could have made the same statement. Not only Canada but other nations have been trying to resolve this problem for many years.
It would be possible, I think, if we wanted to have a completely controlled economy- and I doubt that any of the hon. members directly opposite would favour that-for the government to intrude into the field of private enterprise and create special economic controls which would ensure housing support at all times. But since we have a private enterprise economy I suggest we must strike a balance between the need of funds for housing and the need of funds for other purposes, including social welfare measures, as well as moves to keep the private sector of the economy pulling its weight, for that is where most of our tax revenues come from.
No one would seriously suggest that a person with an income of more than $10,000 a year needs a subsidy. Subsidies are not needed for that type of housing, nor are they needed for luxury travel, for the operation of expensive automobiles, for the purchase of television sets and so on. Surely there is a place in a free enterprise economy for operations of this new interest formula. I say that for those who do not need a subsidy, housing should and must compete with other forms of consumer purchasing. This philosophy was reflected in my announcement last evening of an increase in the maximum permissible N.H.A. rate.
Admittedly-and I make no apologies for it-the new maximum rate will be the highest ever established for lending under the act. But it is a rate which this parliament, or rather a previous parliament, introduced into the act to be used in circumstances such as the present. Make no mistake. Anyone with any knowledge of business in this country will agree that the new rate is a most realistic one in view of the prevailing economic conditions. I might say we have been under heavy pressure for the past year to free the rate entirely. Such action would certainly have given new appeal to N.H.A. mortgages but it is an essential purpose of the act to contain the rate within reasonable boundaries in line with economic conditions, and these
Seplember 28, 1967

Hear, hear.
Supply-Labour

Actual commitments this year already are well in excess of $750 million and up to the end of August more than $500 million had been allocated in direct loans for home ownership and rental housing. This is double the direct assistance that was made available in 1966 which, incidentally, was a record year.
Unfortunately, the rate of expenditure is one which cannot be continued indefinitely, since the allocation of funds for housing must be considered within the framework of the government's total social obligations, in addition to this $500 milliion for direct housing loans, the government has committed very substantial sums to assist in areas of housing which were neglected when hon. members opposite were responsible for the government of the country-areas which did not exist. We have committed substantial sums to those areas of housing where federal authorities have their greatest responsibilities, namely, housing for low income families, housing for senior citizens and students, and loans and grants for urban renewal.
All these activities, regardless of any economic pressures from outside, require vastly increased government programs. It is in this sector that government housing effort is most justified and it is the government's intention to devote a growing portion of federal aid to these vital social aspects of housing.
The following figures will, I believe, be of interest to all hon. members. Nearly $150 million has already been provided this year for public housing projects throughout the ten provinces. A further $21 million has been made available for the construction of low rental accommodation for senior citizens. Almost $54 million has been allocated for student housing. Municipal programs to eliminate blight and enhance general living conditions have been assisted through urban renewal loans and grants totalling upwards of $55 million, while another $29 million has gone to improving municipal sewage facilities. In this field this year more than $300 million has been allocated to areas of the greatest social need-more than the whole annual program of the party opposite when they were in power, more in nine months of the year than they did in their whole program in a full year, including direct loans, I might say.
Hear, hear.

The amendments to the National Housing Act which were approved by parliament in June, 1964, have encouraged provinces to incorporate their own housing

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
corporations or agencies. They had not done so previously. They have organized now to co-operate in programs to provide housing for low income families and the elderly. Since the passing of the revisions in 1964, agencies have been or are being formed in eight out of the ten provinces. The same 1964 amendments opened new opportunities for provincial action in the field of public housing as an alternative, at their option, to joint federal-provincial participation. They offer the provinces long-term low interest loans equal to 90 per cent of the cost of the project. Our low rental homes program has enjoyed marked success as witnessed by the fact that in one province at least 90 per cent of the money they invest is being put up by the federal government. In other cases 75 per cent of the funds is put up by the federal government.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
As a result of this 1964 legislation-and I think these figures are interesting-16,000 public housing units have been placed under the federal-provincial arrangements and under the 90 per cent loan-assisted program. That is 16,000 units in a little over 30 months, as against 11,700 units in the previous 15 years. It is encouraging that we are making progress at this time and bringing the provinces and municipalities actively into the picture, but it has taken enabling legislation to do so.
In addition to the substantial support being given to the public housing programs, I am anxious to expand substantially the activities of limited dividend housing corporations which were active for the first year or two but which seem to have been quietly forgotten in recent years.
During my visit earlier this year to the ten provinces I emphasized that limited dividend housing corporations can effectively provide, with federal or provincial funds, housing for low income families as well as for elderly persons. I have encouraged the provinces, municipalities and charitable organizations to move into this field. I have also undertaken-and this will be implemented promptly-to make the adjustments in rent levels which are permitted, and as well and perhaps more importantly, in the maximum income qualification. This is because a person cannot get a house financed by a limited dividend corporation if he has an income in excess of $5,000. The provinces, after getting advice from the municipalities if they wish to do so, may recommend the rent level that they think appropriate in a particular case.

We all know, Mr. Chairman, that there is no easy answer to the complex problem of housing production and to the allied problems that arise from urban renewal and development. This is particularly true in the metropolitan cities of Canada. I refer not just to Toronto or Montreal or Vancouver or Winnipeg but to cities ranging down in size to the city of Hamilton.
Mr. Chairman, the availability of mortgage funds, while it is a very important factor, is only one factor. Even if we had the market for double the quantity of housing next year as well as the ability to build that number -say 300,000-it would require ancillary services far beyond the capacity of our provinces and municipalities to provide, certainly beyond the capacity of the municipalities.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, there are many problems affecting the production of housing that can be resolved only by local or provincial initiative, including the supply of land, zoning, urban planning and building by-laws.
While there is absolutely no question, as I have readily conceded at the outset, that housing is a matter of grave national concern, I must say that in view of our rapidly expanding population the problem is bound to be with us indefinitely in those areas where growth takes place. For example, Toronto; when I first visited Toronto at the end of the first war it had a population of about 600,000 but it is now nearly four times that size and nearly one-third of its population has come from other countries.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the minister to advise him that the time allotted to him has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to allow the minister to continue?
Agreed.

I thank hon. members for their co-operation. I will not be much longer because I know hon. gentlemen wish to make their contribution and they may have a few questions to ask.
As I way saying, Mr. Chairman, Toronto is perhaps the best example in Canada of situations such as this, partly because of the unusually high percentage of new Canadians who have moved to that city within a relatively short period of time. This situation
September 28, 1967

requires that federal, provincial and municipal governments work together in closest cooperation in order to provide the long-range planning which is necessary to supply the services to meet a greatly enlarged housing program.
We all know perfectly well that in Toronto there are no serviced housing lots available at a price much less than $12,000 per lot. We also know that in some of the municipalities surrounding the city of Toronto the problem is that the town councils would like to see more apartment buildings erected within their boundaries, not individual homes. The reason for this is very simple. More schools are required and the municipalities need money to pay the teachers; yet the major tax base is in the city of Toronto. This is true in every large metropolitan area in the country. There must therefore be joint planning and a joint course of action by the three levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. This is necessary in order to provide for the arterial roads that are needed, serviced lands, schools, churches, shopping facilities and all the other pieces that go to make up our urban fabric.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As I said at the outset, I welcome wholeheartedly this debate because it gives me an opportunity to invite not just criticism-I welcome it and no one should be in public life if he is not prepared to take it; you have to have broad shoulders and take it with a smile-but constructive suggestions from hon. members directed toward a solution of this problem of major national importance. Criticism is relatively easy for partisan politicians, but we want helpful suggestions.
I do not want hon. members to think that this housing problem has not been given a great deal of thought by me and by others. Suggestions have been made by members of the house and representations were made in the first three months of this year while I was visiting the different cities in all parts of Canada that real encouragement would be given to home ownership if the interest portion of mortgage payments, were deductible for income tax purposes. There is nothing new about that. I understand that it was most successful in Germany in the years subsequent to 1948. It has also been suggested to me that speculation in land holdings may be reduced if a capital gains tax or some other technique were used to prevent excessive profits in the disposal of land held for speculation. There are cases where lots were acquired for $1,200 or $1,500 and after sitting
Supply-Labour
there for 10 or 15 years or so are now worth $12,000 or $14,000. Municipalities and provinces are deeply involved in this kind of suggestion, but two of the provinces actually collect income taxes. This type of suggestion deserves very serious consideration but it could not be put into operation without the consent of the provinces.
There are other factors affecting the production and cost of housing which involve the municipalities and provinces in a very real way. It is partly for these reasons that I made a suggestion to the Prime Minister-others may have made it but I know I did some time ago-that some form of federal-provincial discussion take place to enable urban development in Canada to keep pace with requirements in a realistic and practical way. Unfortunately, with three provincial elections going on we are not likely to have this in the next six or eight weeks, I am convinced, however, that such a conference should be held and it should be held this fall if possible. At least it should be held early in the new year if not before the end of this year.
Housing is an area in which all of us regardless of party affiliation share a common concern. Let us have constructive criticism and constructive suggestions during today's debate.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a
question of the minister? In view of the small amount of usage with regard to the loans for existing housing is the minister considering an increase in the amount?

It is under constant review. I might say that as yet the applications we have received for loans do not indicate that there should be an increase in the level of the ceiling. They are coming in now at the rate of about 600 or so a month. The average loan is less than $9,000. There are hundreds, literally tens of thousands, of houses in the Atlantic region, Ontario, Quebec and the prairie provinces where home owners can move to advantage at the present level. We are trying to allocate the amount of money available to help the largest number of people rather than limit the number. Until the program has been in force for at least a number of months, I think it would be unwise to change the ceiling. However, this ceiling is constantly under study.
I believe the minister said that the average amount of the loans is approximately $9,000.

For older houses, yes

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour

Yes. Does the minister understand that there are literally thousands and thousands of people buying homes, for example in Toronto, where the amount of the loan required is far in excess of the maximum loan and that therefore it would be nothing but an exercise in futility to make an application. I would be glad to supply the minister with numerous examples. In view of this, why is the government not now prepared to give consideration to this matter and enact legislation to increase the maximum amount? What is the use of a person applying for a $10,000 loan when he needs $14,000 in order to buy a house?

The answer is simple. We are receiving an increasing number of applications from all parts of Canada. At first when this procedure for loans on existing houses was new people did not know about it, but it is increasing in tempo. That was particularly evident in Winnipeg when I was there discussing housing matters on Monday of this week. I do believe that we should have at least another few months experience before we consider increasing the level.

If it is working there, good luck to them, but what is the use of making an application in an area like Toronto or Ottawa where the loan requirement is $13,000 or $14,000 and the maximum allowance is $10,000. It is ridiculous. Why are you not prepared to increase the maximum amount to $15,000 or $16,000 and see what happens, thereby giving the people in the cities a chance to get in on this legislation?
No answer as usual.

The other day, in relation to his capacity as Minister of Labour, the minister spoke of task forces and anticipatory forces being set up under his direction to probe developing situations on the labour front and to anticipate problems which might appear on the labour front so that there could be planning to meet these problems. I think that statement was enthusiastically received by people all across Canada. My question to the minister at this point simply is, are a similar approach and attitude being brought to bear on this other area of his capacity so that in the future the recurring chronic crises in housing can perhaps be planned for, anticipated and headed off?

There is considerable merit in that suggestion. This is not the first time it

has been made, but it certainly is a meritorious one. I have given very serious thought to recommending that either a committee of this house or of the two houses of parliament study this matter so that their views can be placed before the federal-provincial conference when it is held.
Mr. Chairman, for the first time in this house we have seen a minister who is responsible for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation act in a belligerent way-
Oh, oh.

-in addressing the house. I did not believe the minister had the capability of doing so. I can only say that it must be a camouflage to draw the attention of the Canadian people away from the real crisis in this country in the domain of housing. The minister has endeavoured to go back over the years and refer to the records of previous governments, fully realizing that Canada is a young and growing nation and that the forecast of the experts was that more family units would be formed in the years 1966 to 1970. He goes back to statistics in order to prove that with a population of 20 million the same principle can be applied that applied to a population of 15 million or 16 million.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This is an exercise in futility, Mr. Chairman, which will not answer or solve the serious problem now facing the Canadian nation. There is a serious crisis in Canada and it will not be solved by merely repeating statistics. We must be more realistic and get down to basic thinking. This government has never done that. It seems to be more interested in political expediency than in anything else, and it refuses to stand up and admit to the Canadian people that the position it adopted and followed over a period of three years is one which is now causing the deep concern that all Canadians have today.
The minister knew of the projected estimates and the estimated housing requirements and he has taken action at a snail's pace. By referring to the government's record of ten years ago he has hoped to camouflage the inefficiency of his administration in so far as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned. We do not have to go back very far to see the true picture. Statistics from the Canadian Housing Review show that housing starts declined
September 28, 1967

from an annual rate of 151,000 units last July to 146,000 in August. The house construction industry is normally very active in the summer months, and when we note that in the middle of the summer there is a decline in housing starts we can be sure we are in for a serious disappointment in the fall of the year.
N.H.A. activity in respect of approved loans remained relatively low in August with loan applications in the amount of 877 units. This was 5.1 per cent below the year before in respect of seasonal adjustments. This represents an annual rate of about 10,500 units. With a situation like this in a young, growing country such as ours with so many new families we can expect a disastrous 1968.
The announcement made by the minister last night about the increase in the interest rate was no great surprise to prospective home owners and potential investors. The home owner has come to know this government as one that operates with patch-up legislation, interim measures, ill-conceived, unsuitable and not very well thought out policies for the Canadian people. It is obvious that this announcement was not surprising to potential home owners in view of the criticism which has been levelled at the government over the past few years by those who have aspired to the ownership of shelters. This criticism has been so intensive the government has been forced finally to throw out the challenge to those who supply the source of funds by allowing this fantastic increase in the interest rates.
It is not surprising that the government had to delve deep into the old practices to find justification for increasing the rate to 1 per cent above that which was suggested by the minister some six months ago. The shortage of homes in Canada is reaching such an alarming proportion we are witnessing in our large centres and rural areas great stress and mental suffering on the part of prospective home owners. This is the result of the turmoil into which these people have been thrown by the actions of the government.
Let me refer to a statement made by the minister on April 10, 1967, as recorded at page 14704 of Hansard. In answer to a question that day the Minister of Labour said:
There is no fixed date. It is in line with the return, the long-term yield on government bonds and. as already forecast, it has dropped to 7 per cent. It is the government's hope that there will be a further drop before long under the formula announced last December.
What a formula that was, Mr. Chairman. It resulted in an increase from 7 per cent to 27053-165

The construction industry can be as well employed in building public housing as in building single family dwellings at $20,000 or more, luxury apartments or large office buildings. I believe it is entirely clear that there is no constitutional objection to such a scheme.
I think all of us in the house would agree that public housing is now an urgent necessity. I think we would also agree that it is

not the best ultimate solution. All of us, I am sure, look forward to the day when every healthy Canadian can earn enough money by his own efforts to provide decent housing for himself and his family so that public housing will be required only by the elderly, the sick and the disabled. In the meantime, however, we do have a public housing crisis in some of our large cities. I hope that members of all parties will support additional federal action in this field.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before calling on the next speaker it is my duty, pursuant to standing order 39A, to announce the adjournment proceedings for ten o'clock.

The hon. member for Kootenay West- Power, Columbia river, alleged delay in federal payments to British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, before I make my brief remarks this evening I should like to give my views relating to partisanship. I think partisanship is at its worst when we deal with personalities in the House of Commons in the wrong way. It seems to me there is a new type of partisanship coming from the government this afternoon.
What has been happening, Mr. Chairman? We have been telling the government for three years that there is a housing shortage in Canada and that the government is doing nothing about it. All members who returned to their constituencies this summer discovered there was a housing crisis, not a shortage. We have been putting on Hansard day in and day out for the last three years positive suggestions in the matter of housing. But what has happened? The government and its supporters come to the House of Commons at the resumption of this session in the fall of 1967 and say: "Oh, don't be partisan; don't criticize us."
I suggest that that is exactly the role of an opposition, and we are going to continue to put forward positive suggestions on the floor of this house. We are also going to continue to point out to the people of Canada that this government has no policy and is giving no national leadership in the field of housing. I
September 28, 1967

suppose that the hon. member who has just spoken would accuse me of being partisan in saying that, but I am only saying what every Canadian is saying right now in every part of the country.
Reference has been made to the constitution. Canadians in every corner of the country today are sick and tired of the government hiding behind the constitution. Ten years ago there was absolutely no doubt it was the federal government that was responsible for inflation and the rise in the cost of living, the number one domestic concern today of Canadians. Yet the Minister of Finance rises in this house and says there is doubt about where the constitutional responsibility lies.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Ten years ago, five years ago, when we were in power, there was no doubt in our minds that the provinces and in turn the municipalities had a real role to play in housing policy. There was also no doubt in our minds that housing was a national consideration and concern. Every time we get up on the floor of the house and invoke the government's responsibility, what happens? Is the parliamentary secretary to the minister really serious when he rises and invokes the constitution and tells us it is really a provincial concern? Not at all. Would he go back to his constituency in the face of a housing crisis and wave the constitution in his constituents' faces? I hope not.
Let us be clear now that while we require the co-operation of the provinces and the municipalities the ultimate responsibility for housing or the lack of it, rests with the federal authority. It is passing strange to me that while the government is always talking about the desirability of the central authority, the federal government, being able to have its hands on the various levels of power, the minute the cost of living spirals, the minute there is a problem such as a housing crisis or in respect of urban development, water pollution, air pollution or soil pollution, the minister concerned gets up and says it is not their responsibility but is the responsibility of the provinces.
The hon. member who just spoke said that he was sick and tired of the buck being passed. It is this minister and this government that are passing the buck. We ask the minister and the government not to give us long speeches about interest rates and not to quote statistics but rather to accept their responsibilities and act.
Supply-Labour
I am very glad the minister made the speech he did today. I do not hold the Minister of Labour solely responsible for the housing crisis. It is part and parcel of the bankrupt economic policy of this government. He is forced into this position by the fact that the government has not co-operated with the provinces in planning economic and social priorities. He is forced into this position by the unplanned spending of the government and by the continuing budget deficits. He is forced into the position of high interest rates because the government has not disciplined itself or planned priorities within the national sphere or with the provinces.
I am glad the minister has made it clear that he is not accepting one of the central recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada, namely, that modern government must regard housing as a social welfare matter and must realize that housing is not one of those areas of social welfare which should be affected by normal economic fiscal planning.
Time and time again this government has not paid heed to the positive suggestions from this side of the house. At every session for three years we have told the government that as long as it regards us as a parliament to be played with in conjunction with fiscal and monetary measures it is not going to have a satisfactory housing policy. The minister today turned his back on this suggestion and pinpointed the fact that the Canadian government is the only government in the modern western world which does not regard housing as a social welfare matter and one which should not be affected by the ups and downs of normal monetary fiscal management.
We believe that proper and decent housing is a priority welfare and social matter. With poor housing many other social and welfare programs cannot be brought into effect. Juvenile delinquency and all the urban problems that we need to attack in a positive and constructive way cannot be attacked as long as we are not providing our people, not only in the low but also now in the middle income group, with decent housing. So we consider housing, along with education, a priority item in terms of social welfare matters.
The Liberal party likes to consider itself the pioneer in do-good legislation, but I think they are missing this primary priority because of the whims of fiscal management. I am glad the minister spoke as he did. He gave us a wonderful lecture about how we do not have much housing when the interest rate goes one way, how we do pretty well when it

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
goes another way, and so on. We followed the minister with great care, but in sum and substance he was telling us that he is going to turn back on the main and central recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada. So we will continue to have a housing crisis in this country until there is a change of government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You will wait a long time.

That is one example from the minister's remarks. He belaboured the problem of low-cost land in cities like Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver-all the large metro and urban centres of this country. He spoke of the unavailability of good, low-priced land. We on this side of the house are quite aware of this. Three years ago we told the minister that there was a need to develop co-operation with the municipalities and the provinces whereby low-cost land would be available to the citizens of this country.
The minister points out this problem to us today. I sincerely hope we will not have to have another two years of study before it is pinpointed again. We have been aware of it for three years. I hope the minister does not feel that he has just informed us of it for the first time in the house this afternoon.
One of the reasons which I have already given for the engendering of a high degree of cynicism on the part of the Canadian people toward the federal authority is related to the fact that the federal government far too often when it gets into trouble decides to be partisan and hide behind the constitution. Canadians in every corner of this land are becoming very concerned because no level of government is treating modern problems seriously-some of the problems are not so modern-and no level of government today is seriously confronting the problems of housing, air pollution, water pollution, soil pollution, and urban development.
This is just one instance where a minister of the government is being frustrated. This government will not let parliament and the elected representatives play their part in modernizing and updating our constitution. I am not speaking only of French or English cultural rights in all parts of Canada. It is my view that one of the real causes of national disunity today is related to what I call the real economic issue because the government will not let members on both sides of House of Commons get down to work on modernizing and updating our constitution. Because of this we continue to have such things as housing crises and spiralling costs without any

feeling on the part of the people at the grass roots level that any level of government is effectively tackling these problems.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
What happens then? Month after month, year after year, we in the opposition put positive suggestions on the record of the House of Commons to no avail. Government spokesmen, such as the one today, get up and quote statistics. Today we heard from the minister. Tomorrow I am sure we will hear from his parliamentary secretary, and I can almost quote what he will say. He has made the same speech 50 times. He will invoke the constitution in a manner similar to that of his minister who today gave us a little lecture in economics. He told us that he could not put funds into the economy as long as housing is operating at a certain level.
Let me inform the minister that he cannot hide behind that kind of speech any more. He is going to be faced with this type of criticism until he recognizes that housing is a social welfare matter and that the right to a decent house, a decent dwelling and a decent roof over one's head is a fundamental right in a free, democratic country. The minister made a good nineteenth century speech today, but that is just not good enough for 1967. I would be surprised if his speech today gets much caucus support, particularly if some of the members on that side to whom I have spoken are really serious about where they stand in the political spectrum.
Let me ask simply what the government is going to do to solve this problem. The minister has quoted statistics today, but the fact of life is this. We are at least 50,000 housing units short this year and unless the government does something about this situation it will become worse before it becomes better. Marie Antoinette said "Let them eat cake". What is this government going to say to these people who do not have decent roofs over their heads? Is it going to tell them to get tents? Is the government going into the business of distributing tents in the months ahead? I am not being facetious. It is just not good enough for the government to quote statistics.
The housing crisis does not only exist in the urban and metropolitan districts. Many people in rural districts do not have decent homes today because this government has not evolved a good policy. What is the problem? Basically, at this time Canadians in the lower income brackets are faced with a real crisis. I suggest that people in the middle income
September 28, 1967

bracket are now lacing a real crisis. Many Canadians in the middle income bracket can not And homes to live in today, and this has been pointed out many times. These people are flooding into the cities.
Recent figures show a record upsurge in immigration. Young married couples born in the immediate post-war era are now looking lor homes. The minister invoked the argument this afternoon, which simply does not hold up, that il you talk with young married couples or couples in the middle income bracket you will find that they have made all sorts ol provisions lor travelling, lor education and lor many other things. That is true, but in the minister's lecture this afternoon he stated that these people have not really given priority to or made provision lor the purchase ol homes. That is also true because the cost ol a home is so high it is out ol reach ol the average lamily. These people do not even consider buying a home because houses are so expensive.
As a Conservative, deep down in my heart I believe that home ownership is a great thing. I believe in what might be termed an ownership democracy. I believe in a democracy that encourages people to own their own homes, small businessmen to own their own businesses and larmers to own their own farms. I believe that Canadians should invest more in the shares ol Canadian companies. I believe that the reason people are not talking about owning their own homes is that they are priced so far out of the market today they cannot begin to afford them. A home should not be something just lor the rich.
I think I have said at least three times during this debate, but it must be said again and again, that in a country like Canada which has the second highest standard ol living in the history of the world, it is nothing short ol a disgrace that we should have the kind ol housing crisis that is lacing this nation today. All the minister apparently can do is get up in his place and give the sort ol economic lecture he has given this afternoon, without giving any real encouragement to those people who want a decent roof over their heads. I had hoped for better. I hoped he would give some encouragement this year when we are talking about new and modern politics. All he has done is quote statistics to those who are living in want and deprivation.
Last year in Toronto the average price of a new home was $29,000, yet in 1965 approximately 85 per cent of housing loans financed
Supply-Labour
by the federal government were made to individuals with annual average incomes ol over $5,000. Where does this leave the low income worker? The answer is that it often leaves him living in squalor in run-down metropolitan areas. I do not say this in a demagogic way, but such poverty amongst plenty should be stopped. I hope this is the last time in respect of a subject as sensitive as this that a minister ol the Crown will get up and quote a lot of bureaucratic statistics.
In 1967 housing starts, instead ol increasing over the number in 1966, are beginning to slip badly. We do not have to make speeches about this; this is the fact. The winter season last year was half over when the government recognized this problem, even though week after week we pointed it out to the minister. Day after day, along with members of the N.D.P., we asked what action the minister intended to take.
During a period of time when a great deal of cynicism was being directed at this institution, the minister went on a cross-country lecture tour. You may conduct a parliamentary inquiry or whatever you wish, but one of the real reasons people are getting fed up with much of what is being attempted by the government is that the government has built delaying procedures into our activities. We have had a record number of royal commissions, some of which have been very good; yet only a small percentage of their recommendations has been carried out. The Registrar General is now following this procedure. If a problem develops he suggests that we set up a task force. He will not even face the problem; he sets up a task force.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
When President Kennedy set up a task force in the United States this simply meant that the tentacles of the White House would reach out over the United States. Such a task force was required to report back within a few weeks at the most. If an extension of time was required a very good reason had to be supplied. The very phrase "task force" in the United States denoted the urgency of a problem. Today when we face a crisis in Canada the government sets up a task force which may report in one, two or even three years. If we in the opposition ask why it cannot report sooner, we are shouted down.
A great deal has been said about research. I am not one of those anti-eggheads or antiintellectual individuals. I recognize the real need for research in housing, but what frightens me is that the government may have

September 28. 1967
Supply-Labour
been using research and study as an excuse for delay. There is a time for study but there is also a time for action, even though we do not know or cannot be 100 per cent sure we are right all the time. I am a great believer in computerized research. I believe that in modern government we require more and more research. However, when we are faced with a crisis this government institutes more research when it should in fact be acting. I suggest to the minister that the research he is carrying out now should have been done five years ago. Am I to tell a constituent in my riding that he cannot have a house over his head until we-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You were in power five years ago.
As the hon. member says, we were in power five years ago. This policy might have been good enough at that time.
Oh, oh.

The voting digits from my province are upset. They are becoming exercised now because they have also been told by their constituents that homes are needed. Research is a must, but let us not invoke the need for more research for the purpose of delay, delay, delay.
Last year the minister came up with a new kind of meeting, the symposium. He went across the nation calling housing symposia with the municipalities and provinces. Having gone across the nation calling one symposium after another, he tells us in his speech today that we need yet another federal-provincial meeting before we can have any action. All he did was travel across this country calling symposiums. It was a sort of lecture tour.
The minister told the provincial officials to get off their chairs; he told the muncipalities what they should be doing, always becoming a little irritable in the house when we told him what he should be doing. Now we have not a housing shortage but a housing crisis, and we are still telling him what he should be doing. This afternoon the minister suggested another federal provincial conference before anything can be done. Yet some hon. members wonder why Canadians are getting sick and tired of buck-passing, hiding behind the constitution and the fact that no level of government is facing up to its responsibilities in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question?
The hon. member may certainly ask me a question.

The hon. member for Brome Missisquoi has said that last year the minister spent his time crossing the country calling symposiums. The hon. member for Danforth said the minister was sitting in his office. Both hon. members cannot be right. Is the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi wrong or is the hon. member for Danforth wrong?
Perhaps the minister found time to do both.
And produce nothing.

Housing starts in 1967, instead of increasing over 1966, are falling off badly. The fall of the year is here and we have gone from a housing shortage to a housing crisis. Unless I misunderstood the minister's words, those who are looking for homes cannot take much encouragement from the announcement last night or from the minister's speech in the house this afternoon.
I repeat what I have already said. I believe that every Canadian family should have the right and opportunity to own a home or to enjoy adequate rental accommodation. I agree with the government that this should be brought about in co-operation with private industry and the provincial and municipal authorities. But I do not agree that the federal government does not have the primary responsibility in this regard. A housing crisis is surely a national issue, especially a housing crisis that is spread right across this nation. If it is not a national issue, what are we doing here in Ottawa?
In my view the inability to act on important issues such as this is one real cause of separatism. I do not like to use that word but we all complain today about the power of the provincial governments. This complaint is often heard. We say that the provincial governments are too powerful and the federal government is not allowed to do the things it should do. This is an area in which the federal government should be acting, but it is abdicating its responsibility.
And joking about it.

What about home ownership? It should be encouraged. Just in case hon. members opposite think we have no positive suggestions to put forward I should like to list a few. With respect to home ownership we should be encouraging intensive research into new methods of building lower
September 28, 1967



cost housing and furthering research into cooperative building and ownership. I am talking about the kind of research that we need. The kind of research that has been carried out has inhibited us from acting in other areas. Second, we should eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Third, we should exempt from taxable income an amount up to $500 for school and municipal taxes. Let us consider this suggestion. Is it practical? Perhaps hon. members opposite think it is not. But let us talk about it; it is an idea.
Fourth, we should extend the original Progressive Conservative legislation to provide low-cost, long-term loans to municipalities for sewage treatment projects and other anti-pollution measures. Fifth, we should establish a municipal capital availability fund for purposes of long-term, low-cost loans. We have been suggesting this for years. Now the minister rises in the house and talks about the problem of the unavailability of funds for low-cost loans. Sixth, we should extend direct Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans to include those who today cannot qualify for reasons of income. Seventh, we should increase direct loans on older housing, especially where a housing shortage exists. A little progress has been made in this regard. Eighth, we should make group mortgage insurance available to all N.H.A. mortgage holders.
What about low-cost rental housing? In this connection I make the following suggestions. First, we should provide low-cost, long-term federal loans and a higher federal share of capital costs and operating losses. Second, we should co-operate with the provinces and municipalities in the setting up of minimum standards or ordinances for rented accommodation and provide incentives for both urban and rural municipalities to fight blight and decay in housing by such ordinances. Third, we should provide long-term loans to municipalities for the acquisition of land for housing and/or recreation purposes. This is another answer to the point raised by the minister this afternoon.
Fourth, we should provide such incentives as are fair to encourage the investment of capital in house financing. What the minister said today was true. There are a great many people who are in the building industry to make a profit. I do not think anybody is against that. The facts of life dictate this. I believe that in a realistic way we should encourage a policy that would be an incentive
Supply-Labour
for people to invest capital in house financing.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman but the time allotted to him has expired.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to answer all the questions raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. When he got down to his suggestions at the end of his speech, I thought he was really indicating the program that had been carried out by the Liberal government rather than things that should be done in the future.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I wish to speak briefly in this debate as Acting Minister of Finance in the absence of my colleague, the hon. member for Eglinton, who is attending the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and International Bank in Rio de Janeiro.
All of us in the government recognize the importance of housing in our economic and social policies. It is one of the most essential needs of the people of Canada, a need which will grow and change as our population grows and changes in its composition. The Economic Council of Canada has done us all a service in showing how these needs grow and change in accordance with the growth of the various age groups of the population, as well as noting the influence of increasing incomes on the desire of unattached persons, as distinct from family units, to have accommodation of their own.
The federal government of Canada over the last 35 years have become increasingly and productively involved in the housing situation. Our main activity commenced as a credit measure during the depression, improving notably the source of mortgage funds. When the war was over our operations were considerably extended and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was set up to carry them out vigorously.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Its activities have led the government of Canada into initiating, advocating and supporting a wide variety of programs, from the insuring of mortgages at the one extreme to the support of town planning and urban development at the other. We in parliament can claim some credit. We in parliament have become very conscious of what can be done and should be done through the financial instruments that are available to us.

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
It must be recognized, however, that housing, urban development, land use and all the municipal problems that relate to it, are matters within provincial jurisdiction. Our influence has been important and productive but it cannot be conclusive. As my hon. colleague, the Minister of Labour, has pointed out, there are many things which cannot be done by money in this field. It is important that problems, for example, relating to the supply and use of land, which comes within provincial jurisdiction and the normal responsibilities of municipalities, should be dealt with just as vigorously as the supply of funds for the building of houses. Moreover, as my colleague, the Minister of Finance pointed out some months ago, it is quite important that the effects upon housing of the real property taxes of municipalities be taken into account. He noted in April that, along with other influences, these taxes make house and apartment costs too high. Part of the solution of the housing problem must be found in improving the financing of municipalities.
A good deal of the current problems in housing arise from the shortage of funds in the capital market available for lending on mortgages. Our own experience in Canada in the past, as well as experience in the United States, has shown that housing is vulnerable to competition for funds in the capital market. In part, this vulnerability arises from the greater competitive power of the competing borrowers, dowdy businesses on the one hand and governments and municipalities on the other. In part, it arises from a variety of institutional arrangements including the competitive power of those savings institutions that normally invest in mortgages as compared with those that normally invest in other things. Part of the trouble derives from the nature of the mortgage instrument itself. All of these factors must be considered in looking to any long term solution of the housing problem. A discussion of them would be appropriate at some future time in this house. In regard to the immediate current problem that confronts us, I would like to say a little with regard to the relationship of housing to the flow of savings and the funds that the government can put into housing as compared with other areas.
Last year, in 1966, the competition for funds in the capital market was very intense and the flow of funds from conventional lenders into the mortgage market and thus into housing was considerably reduced.

Since late last autumn there has been quite a substantial expansion in the money supply which has alleviated the tightness in credit conditions generally. Notwithstanding this expansion there has, however, been a substantial increase in long term interest rates, both in the United States and Canada, after a brief decline last winter. In both countries long term interest rates have reached very high levels despite the substantial expansion in the money supply.
These high rates of interest on bonds and mortgages are the result of the action of investors and borrowers in the markets. Investors are demanding high rates for their savings, in part because there are potential borrowers willing to pay such rates and competition permits them. In part, the demands of investors for high rates arise from their concern over the increasing prices and wages in our economies, that is, concern over inflation. So long as investors in the United States and Canada continue to have the attitude they now have toward long term investments in bonds and mortgages, and so long as there are many long term borrowers in the market, we cannot expect to escape these high rates of interest.
A considerable part of the heavy demands upon the capital market this year is the demand of the government of Canada. The net cash requirements of the government over and above its revenues and its normal nonbudgetary receipts this year are very much higher than they have been for many years past, apart from those arising from the large exchange transactions of 1962. This requires the government to borrow very large amounts. Our borrowings are inevitably part of the problems confronting the capital markets in Canada this year. They are part of the competition which is making it difficult to get sufficient money for mortgages to build houses and apartments. Our demands on the market this year, however, are moderated by our ability to reduce our cash balances this year, as the Minister of Finance said we would do in this budget speech on June 1.
In looking forward to the housing situation next year one of the important issues that has to be taken into account is the extent of the competition there will be in the capital market for savings to be used for purposes other than housing. One of these demands will, of course, be the demand of the government of Canada. Moreover, at the beginning of the next fiscal year cash balances will not be as high as they were at the beginning of this fiscal year, so we shall not have as much
September 28, 1967

freedom to meet our requirements through the reduction of our balances.
The government-the treasury board and the cabinet-is now trying very hard to contain our expenditure and lending programs for next year in order to keep our demands on the capital market down to an amount which we feel is reasonable in relation to the other demands on that market. In doing that we will be helping in the best way possible to allow savings to be used for financing the construction of apartment houses and other rental accommodation, which we feel to be urgently needed in the present situation, and for loans for the purchase of homes.
In this current year, when housing remains under pressure because of the competition for savings from other borrowers, we are taking a number of major steps to make it possible to increase the amount of housing units being built.
The first of these was taken some time ago in changing the Bank Act to permit banks to engage in conventional mortgage lending on houses as well as N.H.A. lending. So far this has not had an appreciable effect on the flow of funds into the construction of new houses, but I am told it will an increasing effect as the year progresses and in subsequent years. The banks now are strong competitors for savings and I would expect them to play a role in the financing of housing which is consistent with their outstanding strength as a financial intermediary. It takes time for them to build up their organization for making mortgage loans and to get it fully functioning, but they should be able to play their full part within a few months time.
The second step we took this year was to approve a large direct lending program for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The Minister of Labour has given some figures to illustrate the magnitude of the corporation's program this year. Let me give some figures to illustrate the magnitude of the contribution which the treasury is making to the housing program by way of loans to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I will give you the net figures representing the amount of loans over and above the amount of repayments received. For this current fiscal year we expect these to be over $660 million. This sum is far higher than it has been in any previous year. Last year it was $489 million, the year before that it was $315 million. For the convenience of hon. members, I might insert a table in Hansard at this point giving the figures for the ten years prior to this year.
Supply-Labour
Mr. Chairman, may I have the permission of the committee to insert this table in Hansard?

speechtext: Is it agreed that this table be inserted in Hansard?
Agreed.

speechtext:

These amounts lent to Central Mortgage are used by it for direct loans for home ownership, for loans and partnership investments in public housing, for loans for special housing for old persons, for student residences at universities, for urban development, and other matters. When the figures have been large the bulk of them have been for direct mortgage loans to individuals or builders for the construction of houses.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The government is only able to lend as much as $660 million for housing this year because it had large cash balances at the beginning of the year which can be reduced as the year progresses. Because we cannot repeat this and because we cannot put more strain on the bond market we cannot continue this high rate of lending for direct mortgage loans beyond the current year. We will continue, however, a high rate of lending which will be used, as the Minister of Labour has indicated, for public housing and other special requirements which cannot be financed in the normal way through the market, as home ownership can be.
The third thing we have done this year is to permit N.H.A. insured mortgage loans to be made at any rate of interest up to the maximum permitted by the housing act itself. This very considerable degree of freedom should enable a more competitive market to be established in mortgage lending, with rates varying according to circumstances and market conditions below this maximum. This should help borrowers to get the funds they require from investors in competition with other borrowers. It will, of course, increase

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
the competition experienced by other borrowers in the market, but we feel that this is essential if housing is to receive adequate capital to meet its requirements.
The same amount of competition, though different in form, would occur if by one means or another the federal government increased its own borrowing in order to provide the funds through C.M.H.C. for direct mortgage loans.
I want to emphasize that the government has not set a rate of 8-4 per cent for the interest on N.H.A. mortgages; rather, it has given the market as much freedom as it can, within existing legislation, to determine what rates are appropriate, given the conditions of the market, the situation of each particular case, and the existence of the insurance provided by the housing act. I would hope that in many, if not most, cases the actual rates will be less than the maximum authorized by parliament in the act, but we cannot be sure until we see the way the market reacts over the next few months.
The fourth step, which the government has not yet taken but has indicated as its intention, is to set in motion a serious study of urban development as a whole and of housing as one element of that development. It will be recalled that in the throne speech the Governor General stated the intention of the government to propose to the provinces that a special study of urban development be undertaken in close consultation with all the authorities concerned, and which would be of assistance to federal and provincial governments and municipalities as well as to the public generally.
In August, the Prime Minister indicated that this conference on housing was something on which we would be getting in touch with the provinces and this would be one of the most important subjects on which consultation with the provincial governments would be necessary. That is still our intention, although, as hon. members will be well aware, with elections taking place in other provinces it will be necessary to wait at least some weeks before provincial governments can be expected to participate in such discussions on this or, indeed, other matters.
I have indicated, as my hon. friend the Minister of Labour has indicated, that the housing problem is not simply one of money. Much else is involved, and almost all those other factors involved are ones within the jurisdiction of the provinces and involve very substantially the actions and financing of municipalities.
Could I ask the minister, if he has a spare copy of the table he placed on Hansard to let me have one.
