speechtext:
The hon. member for
Sudbury.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me the opportunity to contribute to this important debate. I must also thank the government for giving us a choice of crises. We could choose between housing, wheat or the two nations concept. I wonder if that situation will continue throughout the sitting.
It will get worse.

I was surprised at the attitude of the Minister of Labour in the house today. When I met him in Sudbury garnering votes he took a more benevolent attitude toward housing. He was most sympathetic at that time. His position seems to have hardened since then-mind you, he was on another mission.
I agree with his statement that housing subsidies should not be granted to those with incomes of over $10,000. If that is his attitude, why does he not make sure that government funds are used only to subsidize those who need subsidization. I agree that anyone earning $10,000 a year is strong enough to go to the open market for his funds.
I object to his assertion that the new maximum interest rate of 8.1 per cent for mortgages is realistic. It is only realistic if one thinks that housing funds should come entirely from the free market. I do not intend to accept that concept, nor do I think that housing should be at the whim of the free market. It is too important a social aspect to be at the whim of the market.
I must refute what some hon. members of the house may think. The hon. member for St. Paul's thinks that I am making these criticisms in order to make political capital. I am not trying to make political capital tonight, and I did not come to this house for that purpose. Tonight, I am here as a victim of the poor administration of this government, so far as housing is concerned.
September 28, 1967

The minister also criticized the high prices of lots in the city of Toronto, saying that serviced lots at $12,000 were too expensive for individuals to build houses on. I am in sympathy with that sentiment, but I remind him that the problem of land speculation is not new; it has been taking place on this continent for hundreds of years. Abraham Lincoln once said that no man should own or control more land than he needs to raise his family, or conduct his legitimate business. That is my attitude on land speculation. What does the minister intend to do if he is critical about land prices? Will he do something to control land speculation?
I am also surprised that hon. members here should be amazed that we have a housing crisis on our hands today. We knew about the post-war baby boom. We have watched that population grow; we have watched them pass through primary school, secondary school and university. Now, when they are in the housing market we are surprised. Surely, all that could have been predicted. Surely we could have taken steps and made preparations for those we knew were coming. This post-war population bulge is not new. It has been with us for 25 years.
When the minister hides behind the barrier of the constitution, his position is transparent. It is pretty difficult for me to go home and hand the people a copy of the constitution saying, "Here, you can hide under this to get out of the rain." So long as the federal government controls monetary policy in Canada, so long must they accept responsibility for housing. It is of social importance and much too big for municipalities or provincial governments alone.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
It is clear from the evidence we have that the turning on and off of the monetary tap has produced a direct effect on housing starts in Canada. In 1965, monetary restraint led to a decline in housing starts which became apparent in 1966. Here we are, in 1967, still suffering from the effects of that policy.
I always had the impression that government funds should be directed to those people who lacked the financial strength to acquire money on the open market, particularly since the institution of guaranteed C.M.H.C. loans. However, in 1965 only 9 per cent of borrowers were in income brackets below $5,000 a year and in 1966 the situation was even worse-only 4.8 per cent of borrowers found themselves in those brackets. Yet these are the very people who most need help by way
Supply-Labour
of government subsidy. It is not the people who are living on $10,000 a year who need it; they have the financial strength to help themselves. The government should be doing something to subsidize high interest rates on behalf of those in the low income brackets.
I take objection to the minister's statement that the problem is one which arises only in the large urban centres such as Toronto, Vancouver and Hamilton. I come from a part of Canada which is off the beaten track. I live in a mining community which does not have a loud voice in parliament. It has become almost a historical fact that people who are miners must endure poor housing conditions. The people of Sudbury are miners, that is a certainty, and I represent them because I am one of them; I have sympathy for them. They are a hard-working people and they deserve more out of life than they have been getting.
In a one-industry community such as Sudbury, financial shocks are not dispersed among a large population as is the case in densely populated metropolitan areas. Whenever something happens to that one industry, everyone gets a severe financial jolt. Living in Sudbury is like riding at the back of a bus, enduring a series of jolts as the economy passes through phases of boom and bust. Right now we are in a boom period economically. Yet though tremendous wealth is generated by the labours of those who often go underground before daylight and do not come up until after dark, we have not discovered a system which will turn this wealth into housing and services for those working people.
I am here tonight to ask the minister to have mercy on these people who labour so hard for so small a reward. The national scene has been covered most adequately by my hon. friend from Danforth. To bring home the true picture to the minister and show him how people are suffering as a result of government policy, I should like to deal with the local situation as I know it to be in the city of Sudbury. I do not know it from the standpoint of academic research; I know it as a long time resident and worker in the city.
Recently, a somewhat famous politician from Toronto, Dr. Morton Shulman, made certain statements about Sudbury. He said it was a slum town and that there was a pall of black smoke hanging over it. I do not necessarily reject entirely Dr. Shulman's assessment of the city of Sudbury. I reject it to an extent; he should have said that only 20 per

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
cent of the city of Sudbury consists of slums. There are some, the elite, the mine managers, the insurance company executives, who live well. But the average miner does not live well and the house in which he lives is part of the 20 per cent described as slums.
This classification is not a random one; the case has been documented by our city planner, whose staff has visited every home in Sudbury. On the streets of Sudbury there are 400 tarpaper shacks. This is not a "guesti-mate", it is the result of an actual count. These shacks were built about 40 years ago, probably, when the success of mining in the areas was touch and go and no one wanted to invest money permanently in housing. They were built to serve a need; they are still there today, and people are living in them.
To make up for the natural decay in housing stocks we need 600 new houses a year. For one reason or another, mostly financial, we have not reached that figure since 1962. One reason for this failure is that we face the third highest building costs in Canada. Instead of having developers in Sudbury we have peddlers-they make a deal and diddle around with land, then they go to Toronto or Ottawa and peddle their programs.
May I call it seven o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being seven o'clock, I do now leave the chair.
At seven o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, before the dinner recess I was attempting to cite how one city suffers from the housing situation, which up to now has been treated on a national or more general basis. As the representative of Sudbury, and realizing that my constituents have had no voice in this parliament for quite some time, I think it is important to bring to this committee the local situation so that hon. members may be apprised of the conditions in the city that I represent.
I was recounting to the committee the housing needs and conditions as they presently exist in the city of Sudbury. I think I stated that we needed 600 houses a year just to offset natural decay caused by age. Then I went on to say that we enjoy-or otherwise-the third highest building costs in Canada, and I believe this is one of the reasons that Sudbury is suffering more acutely than most other cities in Canada.

I should also tell the committee about some of the distress caused by this housing shortage. Quite recently a report delivered by the local children's aid society cited a case where a man and wife and their two children were living in an abandoned automobile on the streets of the city. Other cases cited were of families that had been broken up for no other reason than that the parents could not supply the children with the necessary accommodation. These are not families the heads of which are bums or derelicts, but people who go to work every day and contribute to our society and the wealth of the nickel mines, yet cannot find the wherewithal to supply family needs. As a result, the children in these families have become a charge against the state. I think it is a false economy when we save money by withholding housing on the one hand and handing out welfare on the other.
There is also overcrowding and doubling up of families. The pressure on rents is becoming acute and they are rising to prohibitive levels. In the city of Sudbury it is possible to pay $175 for a four-room frame house. Such a house when built was probably not worth $500, it is being rented today at this price. Others, consisting of only four rooms and a path, rent for $150. I suggest it is a crime in this day and age that the city of Sudbury should be called upon to spend the sum of $14,000 a year and upwards on night soil collection to meet housing needs today, but that is the situation and it is going from bad to worse.
What is projected for the future, Mr. Chairman? I told you about the mining corporations in Sudbury. The two companies have announced-and this is on record-that within the next two and a half years they will require 3,500 additional employees. The International Nickel Company announced two days ago that they could use an additional 1,000 men, and they still need them tonight. Why are they unable to get these employees? It is mainly because housing accommodation is so tight that these people cannot or will not come to the city, plus the fact that the wage rate for these employees is such that they cannot qualify for a mortgage under the restricted plan of the government.
In addition to the 3,500 new employees which are required in the city, we also have to accommodate the service trades. For this purpose we use a multiplying factor of 1.6, which means that for eaoh worker in the city 1.6 men are required by the service trades.
September 28, 1967

This accounts for a further 5,600 new employees in the city. This amounts to a grand total increased population of 8,100, or an increase of 10 per cent in the population over a 30-month period.
There is not one empty bed in the city tonight and yet 8,100 workers and their families are coming to the city. We have been aware of this situation for six or eight months now. The mining companies made this prediction, and the minister was in the city when it was made. Yet the situation has deteriorated in the five months since his visit; nothing has happened to meet the situation.
To give the committee an idea how tight the situation is, Mr. Chairman, hon. members are all familiar with the housing problem in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Or perhaps I should rise on a point of order. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting that we knew this five or six months ago. We heard about it in June approximately; the hon. member knows that.

I beg to differ with the minister. This announcement was made during the election campaign. The by-election was in May and the minister was in Sudbury during that month. It was at that time these figures were first projected by the nickel companies.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We should bear down a little on this subject, since the minister has shown some interest in it. At that time the minister did recognize that we had a problem. Without any urging on our part he announced that he would go to the mining companies to ask them to put up funds to supply us with 150 housing units. He asked the mining companies whether they could put up the funds or consider borrowing the money and making it available to supply 150 rental housing units. That is how serious the minister considered the situation at the time. However, that was during an election period and it is quite easy to get the interest of the minister at a time like that.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. When an hon. member makes statements like that which are not true, I must rise on a point of order. I said after the election, not before, that I had made an approach to the companies. I told them that with their expected help we could be assured of provincial help. There should be no suggestion at all that politics were being
Supply-Labour
played, because this was deliberately done after the election.

Well, Mr. Chairman, this
brings me to the point I should like to raise with the minister. We have waited patiently in the city of Sudbury to see the results of his inquiry of the mining companies. It was not our suggestion that a minister of the crown should go begging to the International Nickel Company for funds. I guarantee that the New Democratic party would deal differently with this company. Of his own volition he did see fit to ask the two mining companies for funds. We have not heard from the minister since that day. I wish he would rise in his place and tell us what the reactions of the mining companies were to his request that they supply the funds to build 150 rental housing units. We need this desperately and we would even accept it from them at this moment.

I would be pleased to give the answer at any time. The answer was a highly satisfactory one. The hon. member will recall that, when I sat down with the mayor and those who had invited me to come to Sudbury, I discussed the problem and said that obviously more public housing was involved and they could accept the assurance of the federal government that I was confident we would get the co-operation of the Ontario government. I also said that, in addition to public housing, other houses were needed and that I felt that the companies concerned might make a contribution over and above what would be done by the federal and provincial governments.
I reported after the election-not during the election-and I then announced that I had received an assurance of full co-operation from the government of Ontario, that we were going to put in the number of public housing units that were needed in the year 1967 according to our estimates. In addition, the mining companies concerned were going to do their part. I said that some 800 starts would be made on houses this year. So, I must take exception when I hear a supposedly responsible member make outrageous statements like those made here tonight.

I take exception to the statement that the statements are irresponsible. I ask again how much money the International Nickel Company and the Falconbridge Mines have put up since the minister made his request of these people.

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
I simply said that the companies would make the arrangements for the housing starts which were necessary in excess of the public housing units that we had originally suggested.

1 must differ with the minister because he promised us that he would increase our housing units from 400 to 800. I was a member of the housing committee in the city of Sudbury. I am an alderman there. We held a meeting of the housing committee three days ago. The housing starts this year will not exceed 600. That is the reason I have waited to see what the mining companies propose to do. Are they going to raise the number from 600 to 800? The mayor has not heard from the mining companies. The city planner does not know, the clerk-controller does not know and I do not know. Apparently the minister knows something and will not tell us.
A mining town is populated largely by working people. There is probably no other industry which employs so much low cost manpower. Therefore, we have a large percentage of low income working people. The average wage for 1965, which is the latest figure I could find in our library, is $5,175 a year. If I were to project the wage increase which we have negotiated with the mines, I would arrive at a figure of between $6,000 and $6,200 a year as the average wage in the city of Sudbury as of tonight. This is only my projection. I could not obtain any closer evaluation.
The new interest rate of 8J per cent will mean that a large percentage of the people in the city will not be in a position to apply for a government sponsored loan. This acute increase in interest rates can only aggravate our housing situation in the city. In fact, when the interest rate was increased the last time to the per cent figure our provincial member for Sudbury stated publicly in the press that he was ashamed to be a Liberal. I myself am ashamed that he is a Liberal. That was his statement. I understand that Mr. Nixon, the Liberal leader in Ontario, is quite upset about the new interest rate.
It is difficult for me, as an amateur politician, to try to follow the devious and dubious tactics carried on by this Liberal government. So, Mr. Chairman, I am reluctant to go back home. The people there have expected me to do great things down here. After 46 years of Liberal rule, they said, "Go down and tell these people something, have a little chat with them". I hope I have done that tonight.

All I can do is go back and tell my people, "You must bleed a little more and suffer a little more, but you still must get up at five o'clock in the morning, go down and moil in the bowels of the earth and when you come back you will live in your little shack and be satisfied." This seems to be the arrogant attitude of the government tonight.
I think it is unfair and unrealistic that the wealth produced from the natural resources of Canada cannot be converted into houses. It is the job of this government and this minister to find ways and means to supply the wherewithal so that these people-not only the people in the poor districts of northern Ontario who know they have been in the back seat of the bus for a long time-can have decent living. So far as I am concerned I cannot sit still and watch this situation continue. So, I will go back to my people and report to them on the position of the government and the minister.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to participate in this debate and I am pleased the Minister is in his seat. He is a congenial sort of fellow and I feel sorry for him because of the position in which he finds himself as a result of the housing situation in this nation.
On a question of personal privilege, Mr. Chairman, may I say that it is rather nice to hear what the hon. member has to say today, after being accused of belligerency earlier this afternoon.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman and Mr. Minister. I do not wish to go over all the points raised by other members this afternoon. I shall attempt to put my remarks in the form of a summary.
After listening very closely to the various speeches, I decided to bring out some information on housing which has not as yet been covered. I doubt whether there is any question in the mind of anyone on this side of the house or in the minds of very few on the other side that the policies followed by this government in respect of housing have not been successful. I believe the minister would be the first one to admit that fact.
Perhaps I could have the attention of the minister if whoever it is who is talking to him would get out of the way. I am talking to the minister.

Speak to the Chair.
Sepiember 28, 1967

I am talking to the minister through the Chair. If the other fellow has not enough courtesy to get back in his own seat, I shall have to tell him to do so.
First of all the bank interest rate was changed. At that time the minister argued that an increased bank interest rate would encourage the banks to get into this housing field. He felt that this, in itself, would help to solve the housing problem. That has not been the case. I remember the argument advanced by the Minister of Labour when he increased the rate of 7J per cent. At that time I did not seriously object, but I felt that what he was doing would not solve the housing problem. Obviously it did not solve that problem.
The minister has now increased the interest rate to 8J per cent. Let me go one step further and suggest that this will not solve the housing problem. The minister is on the wrong track or in a dry hole. He would be far better off to pull up his drill and start on a new hole. In other words, the economic tactics the minister is using to solve the housing problem in Canada will not provide a solution to the situation. I am sure the Minister of Labour and those who sit on the opposite side of the house will join with me in the suggestion that these policies have not worked and will not work. It is time to begin something new.
Everyone knows that if you are going to have adequate housing in this country you must have sufficient finances. Money is still the major problem. The money lenders have this whole situation tied up so tight we are not going to have housing development in Canada if we rely upon our present banks and lending institutions. These institutions provide some of the required funds but they do not provide enough.
We on this side of the house have said on more than one occasion that we must work toward some sort of project development. The minister has referred to urban areas where there is a great deal of new development, including Vancouver and Toronto. One might well mention several others which are rapidly growing centres, like Calgary, Edmonton and so on. In these areas people want housing but are unable to obtain loans. How are they going to get them? The only way one can build a house is by having enough money to pay for it, or by obtaining a mortgage. The government must adopt some type of program to help, but so far government programs have not met the need by increasing the interest rates private lending companies are allowed to charge.
Supply-Labour

Would the hon. member
permit a question?

I would be glad to answer your question a little later. I do not wish to use up too much of my time in that way now. Perhaps what I intend to say at this time will give the minister some clarification. We must find money for housing development, but how are we going to find it? It must be provided through government borrowing, or by the establishment of an institution such as the Industrial Development Bank. That institution, which is associated with the Bank of Canada, has helped start many industries throughout the country. As an economist, I have given some assistance in the development of these industries by helping these people to obtain loans through the I.D.B. I am sure the money involved in helping these industries start, on a high risk basis, has not added to the inflationary trend in this country. Neither has this lowered, increased or depreciated the value of the dollar. Whenever you put new money into the lending streams in the country through institutions such as the Bank of Canada you have to be very careful to maintain a proper balance. There is no way this minister or anyone else can show me how this problem can be solved unless we provide federal capital.
There is nothing wrong with the government providing capital for this purpose. This has been done in times of war and it can be done for the purposes of meeting the housing crisis through a housing development bank similar to the Industrial Development Bank. I am not concerned with the name, but it could have the authority to start projects in the various areas where there is an acute housing shortage. This institution could then start housing development projects in various areas.
The standards for these housing projects should be high and not 20 houses on a one acre plot with buildings almost touching each other. Surely, there is enough land in this country that we do not have to do that. Let me also say to the minister, in the event that he is mistaken about the possibility of such developments, that I was in the state of Virginia some time ago where a housing project was being developed with toilet facilities and the like. Many splendid houses were being built. Unfortunately Senator Bird came along and suggested that these houses were too expensive, and to lower the expense, outside plumbing was provided. Since then this outdoor plumbing has been called "Bird

September 28. 1967
Supply-Labour
houses". I should not like to see here in Canada a similar development called "Nicholson houses".
It is my suggestion that the government should participate in housing projects of type similar to the Teron development on the outskirts of the city of Ottawa. If any of you have not seen this development I suggest that you do so. The minister, instead of obtaining a group of planners to do a great deal of research, should obtain the services of some practical man like Teron, put him on the payroll and turn him loose to develop some of these projects. Mr. Teron has said that he could build these houses for $12,000 to $15,000 including landscaping, sewage and water, etc. These would be two and three bedroom units. If Mr. Teron can do this, I venture to say that the federal government could also do likewise. Certainly it is possible for this government to start housing projects of this kind under a housing authority, by making funds available at a low rate of interest. After these projects were completed, the government could then sell them to the individual, thereby turning them over for private ownership.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Instead of charging $9,000 for a piece of land on which to build a house, instead of saddling the newly married couple that wants to get a start in the world with a $9,000 lot, would it not be infinitely better for this parliament to give the government approval to buy the land and develop it in all areas where there is a critical housing situation? There need not be many projects, but there would have to be enough in order to take up the slack for the time being. If this were done, private lending money, with the contribution of the banks and the support of the government, would ameliorate the housing situation.
There is no other way in which this problem can be solved. I look the minister straight in the eye and defy him to tell me any other method that will solve the housing problem. The minister thinks he will solve the housing problem by manipulating the interest rate and then relying on the banks to lend more money. I would not rely on banks but instead, would set up a corporation that would do the job that is needed for the people of Canada. I am not a socialist-
Hear, hear.

-but I believe that if we must have housing development we must also have

the right kind of organization and the financial backing necessary in order to solve this problem. There is no sense wasting a great deal of time talking about other things. I could talk at great length about the business cycle. The business cycle, which is the reason for the attitude of the banks, is what largely prevents them from making long term loans. The minister cannot deny that. The banks are scared to put their money into long term securities. They have long been accustomed to making short term loans of six months or less, or a year at the maximum. They are not interested in putting their money into projects which will take 15, 20 or 25 years to be paid off.
This is the position in which we find ourselves with respect to the business cycle. This, in addition to other economic factors, has scared the banks away from making long term loans. The minister may, by raising the interest rate to 8j per cent, bring a few more dollars into this field but he will not solve the housing problem in this way. Mr. Chairman, I have probably talked more than I should. I want to give everybody else a chance to speak on this subject. Also, I want to give the minister an opportunity to ask me the question he wanted to ask a few minutes ago.

Mr. Chairman, I was going
to ask the hon. member if he knows how the relatively insignificant amount advanced by the Industrial Development Bank to which he referred compares with the $900 million put into housing this year by the government, but I will not ask him.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister whether he has any figures in this respect. What was the figure put into housing this year by the government?
The budget exceeds $900 million for the year.
That is the government's contribution?

That is the government's allocation, and well over $700 million has already been committed this year. I ask the hon. member, how does that figure compare with the I.D.B. figure to which he has referred, or has he the I.D.B. figure?

That is the amount of money lent for the building of houses. If the government can provide this amount of money with which to build houses, what is the difference? The government should see to it that enough
September 28, 1967

money is provided with which to build the houses that are needed. What would this do to the economy of this country? It would not have any ill effects. There would be no inflation as a result of it. Don't kid yourself about that. If the figure the minister has suggested is correct, and this amount is being put into house construction, it is certainly not the sole cause of inflation.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I thought the hon. member had finished his remarks. Rather than ask him another question, I would simply suggest that he read the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue which will appear in Hansard tomorrow. The minister contributed much to the debate this afternoon and I think he answered the questions that have been raised by the hon. member. This was a supplementary speech, not a question.
Mr. Chairman, I did not hear the last remark of the minister.
I said that, in my opinion, his statement was a supplementary speech.
Are you the chairman?
I rose on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I enter this debate on housing with a great deal of interest. Hon. members have been pointing out the seriousness of this situation. It is a serious situation, but this government and the minister in charge of housing have shown a great deal of concern for the people of Canada.
Abraham Lincoln once said that you cannot establish security on borrowed money. This government has shown responsibility in this area, and at the same time it has shown concern for Mr. Average Canadian Citizen.
And the lumberman.

Supply-Labour
Now that the lot is completely serviced, the contractor can commence building a modest home.
The hon. member missed a paragraph.
Which paragraph did I miss?
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? First, where did he get his figures, and second, can he provide an indication as to how the federal government proposes to reduce these costs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Let him finish his speech. He may get there yet.

I calculated these figures from practical experience. I am not interested in indicating how the federal government is going to reduce this cost because I realize this is a municipal affair. This afternoon the hon. member for Danforth said that the federal government was responsible for the high cost of housing. I recognize this is a municipal affair, and I realize the municipalities must deal with the provincial governments.
Now that the lot is completely serviced, the contractor can commence to build a modest home. Suppose the contractor erects a 1,200 square foot home on this $6,000 lot. What has happened to the cost of this home? First, the building materials have increased in value by about 5 per cent since January 1966. In the province of Ontario 2 per cent of this increase was caused by the Ontario government's increase of the sales tax on building materials from 3 per cent to 5 per cent.
What about the 11 per cent sales tax?

Let us suppose that a 1,200 square foot home were to cost $10 per square foot to build in January 1966. At this stage we would add the extra 5 per cent increase in the cost of materials, so that the home would cost $12,600.
The hon. member is leaving out altogether the 11 per cent tax on building materials.

I will bring in the 11 per cent a little later. I can speak on that also, but I want to leave it until the end.
The second most important cost factor in this home is the increase in the cost of labour, both skilled and unskilled. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, since January 1966 the cost of labour has increased by 29

per cent, so this would add another $1,200 to the cost of the home. It would now cost the contractor $13,800 plus the cost of the serviced lot.
The third major cost to the contractor is interest costs, administration and overhead. These costs have also increased, so we would add an additional $1,500 to the cost of the home. It would now cost roughly $15,300, plus the cost of the serviced lot.

Mr. Chairman, it is fitting that as a member representing the Canadian metropolis, I should express certain thoughts on the problem before us, namely the housing situation throughout Canada and especially in the city of Montreal and in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I want to say to the member for Middlesex East (Mr. Lind), who just resumed his seat, that I intend to reply to his statement about the non-participation of the government of Quebec in the program of urban development, construction of new houses or slum clearance.
If the hon. member for Middlesex East will kindly remain in his seat, I intend to enlighten him about facts he might not have been

DEBATES	September 28. 1967
aware of and it is obvious that he was not because when reading his text he did not know where to put a full stop. I would have told him that if the province of Quebec did not participate with the federal government on a large scale in urban renewal or housing projects in the province of Quebec it is because from 1960 to 1966 a Liberal government was in office there and in the field of housing it failed completely to meet its obligations toward the population. It was necessary to wait until the coming to power of the Union Nationale government, when, through its minister of municipal affairs, Hon. Paul Dozois, it reached an agreement with the present government and set up the Quebec Housing Corporation.
Were the remarks of the member for Middlesex East as encouraging for his party as the minister believes them to be, he should then have told us, and insisted on the fact, that there is a current housing shortage in Canada of some 300,000 units. That is to say, some 300,000 families will have to wait till the minister realizes the housing situation is serious in Canada.
The minister asked us this afternoon,-and I feel sorry for him-asked us, of the opposition, actually to do his work. He told us: I ask the opposition not to criticize the minister, not to criticize the government; I ask the opposition to make suggestions to us.
In all the years I have been sitting here, I have never heard a minister admit so candidly his incompetence, his inability to manage the affairs of his department.
We are not here to bestow flattery on the minister or to express thanks to the government. Indeed, I do not think there should be even one Canadian who should feel compelled to say "thank you" to any government; for we are not here to get thanks but just to see that problems are solved. That is the reason why we have been elected by the people.
It is not difficult for the government or for the minister to say, as the latter said this afternoon: What can we do? The housing situation is serious.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)

I want to quote the minister at this point. He said, if I remember his words correctly, that any country growing as fast as Canada was bound to have a housing problem and that the government was dealing with this problem as it arises. This means that the
September 28, 1967

minister has a 24-hour policy to deal with these urgent matters. He does not attempt to forecast the amount of increased housing which is required by a growing population; he tells the people of this country that he and the government intend to settle these difficulties as they arise.
I would not like to be labelled as a member of a 24-hour policy government, though I think this is the kind of government we have had during the last six years. This is why we are running, as my hon. friend from Bow River said, from crisis to crisis. I say it shows lack of a sense of responsibility. Moreover, when the minister tells us that this is a situation which has only just arisen, he is not speaking in accordance with the facts.
Two years ago, in 1965, La Presse of Montreal, another well known paper Le Devoir and even the Gazette printed articles in the month of January underlining the urgent need for action in the field of housing by the present government. This was two years ago, so the situation has not arisen overnight as the minister suggested. The excuse made by the minister in this regard cannot be accepted by us.
I recognize the hon. gentleman's difficulty. His colleagues across the way think that power is theirs to own as of right until they grow old and retire. I do not agree that this is the case, but because of complacency on their part they are not putting their full weight into the execution of their duties. As an example, let me remind hon. members that the minister told us this afternoon that the problem was not so much a lack of houses as the presence of too many people in this country. I wonder what the Minister of National Health and Welfare would say about that. I think it would be more appropriate for him to convey to his colleague responsible for housing the idea that what we need is not a housing policy but birth control pills for the Canadian people.
These are the kind of arguments used by the minister this afternoon. I am sure they do not suggest answers of the kind the Canadian people want at the present time. I am not speaking in any partisan way; I am speaking for those many thousands of people who are wondering what is to happen to them tomorrow in the area of housing activity. It is because this matter is so serious that we asked early this week for an immediate debate on the subject. The government was not ready; they had not written out their speeches. The hon. member for Middlesex East has just read us his own. I would not
Supply-Labour
have thought it necessary to force the government to take action with regard to housing. The minister promised us that by 1970 there would be 200,000 units of new housing in this country. If we can judge from past promises and the results of last year when the number of units built declined by 32,000, I do not think we can rely on the promises the minister made today in this regard. The situation is so serious that people from all walks of life and in all sectors of activity have for months, if not for years, been telling the government about its urgency.
I can understand the bewilderment the public must now feel, because, like me, they may have been reading the pamphlet which the Liberals put out across the country during the election campaign. The first article in this pamphlet says the Liberal government is determined to "fight the poverty which unfortunately still exists in some areas despite general prosperity". The writer adds: "The plan is ready".
Is the plan ready, Mr. Chairman? Can the minister tell us whether the fight against poverty involves the lack of housing? Does it mean a constriction of the funds available to working class people for the purchase of homes? Members of this house are asking whether the minister really told the truth during that campaign or whether what was said then was merely part of a political propaganda offensive.

Mr. Chairman, housing gives rise to a problem which is so serious that the reports of the Economic Council of Canada, whether it be the third review of November 1966 or that of September 1967, show the seriousness and the importance of this matter.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I know that this has probably been mentioned by other members, but I still want to stress it and draw it to the attention of a government which, it seems, does not intend to consider and read the considerations published in the report of the Economic Council of Canada.
I would like the hon. minister to heed what the Economic Council of Canada has to say in its fourth report which was distributed to us recently. Chapter 9 is entitled "Policy Implications" and deals with the economic policy and policies to assure an adequate expansion of housing. Under that chapter it is stated that:
Of all the major sectors of the economy, none will have to grow more rapidly than housing- at least to 1970, and perhaps even throughout the

September 28. 1967
Supply-Labour
1970's. This is a matter of major national importance if a growing housing shortage is not to become a serious national problem.
Greatly increased physical resources will therefore be required in this field, including a substantially enlarged working force with appropriate skills and considerably enlarged capital and residential construction capacity. A large and sustained volume of residential mortgage financing will also be required.
Here are the exact words of the report which cost a great deal of money to the Canadian people and which points out to the government and the minister responsible for housing the seriousness of the situation and the ways of correcting it.
Mr. Chairman, the report continues by warning legislators against the tendency to use this industry as a cyclical readjustment factor. As a matter of fact, one can read:
The use of housing as an economic regulator should not be continued to such an extent in the future.
This means, obviously, that housing, housing credit and the administration of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have always been linked to the needs, the economic incentive which was necessary for the government to keep abreast and avoid a widespread depression. We are warned against this practice.
I fully agree with this report because there is a growing awareness of the fact that the housing factor is no longer an economic regulator; it has become a factor in itself, a social factor, and a most urgent one.
If we do not settle this problem, if the government beats around the bush, tries to find excuses and defers its decisions, well, Mr. Chairman, we will not be surprised to note before long perhaps a very unfavourable reaction of the people to the government and the confidence that the people should place in their administrators.
The minister is fully aware that the Economic Council of Canada is not the only one to have cautioned him against the present situation; it also happens that briefs have been submitted to him from all quarters.
As an example, I should like to mention the one published in the press recently by the provincial Association of Quebec Home Builders Incorporated. In a press release that I take the liberty of quoting, the president of that important association cautioned the government against the situation which is facing us today.

In the past two years-

Mr. Chairman, I end my quotation here to show the minister that if I quoted those words, it was to point out to him that the problem has been with us for two years and that the government has been helpless or unconcerned in the face of a situation which was growing worse from day to day.
Evidently, arguments have been put forward to the effect that there was also, in the field of housing, a provincial and municipal responsibility. We all recognize the responsibility of the lower levels of government in that field. Indeed, the Ontario government recognized it by creating its own organization; the Newfoundland government also set up its own agency and recently, the Quebec government established the Quebec Housing Corporation, an act which came into force yesterday.
If we admit that the provincial and municipal authorities are responsible in the field of housing, that is no excuse for the inertia, the incompetence and the inability of the minister to see to it that those lower levels of government accept and assume their responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, like some of my colleagues, when I see in my riding families who live in crowded tenements, in dusty cities, in houses which can be destroyed overnight by fire_______I

was unfortunate enough to witness such a fire where two children I knew very well died-I cannot but feel sorry about the fate of those people. That is why I think the federal government, whose responsibility it is to co-ordinate action, to incite-if the minister will accept that word-to stimulate, to wake up the lower levels of government if they will not assume their responsibilities in that field, should do something all the same.
It is quite obvious, Mr. Chairman, that the province of Quebec has not yet, as it ought to have done, taken adequate steps to alleviate the appalling housing conditions which prevail. As the representative of a city of almost two million people or over, I just cannot accept the fact that in a section covering hardly two square miles, there should be over
80,000	people who are more or less decently housed and of whom at least 50,000 live in decrepit houses or lodgings. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that the province of Quebec could have done much better than it has to date for, of the 12,000 emits-

Many factors are responsible for the present housing shortage across Canada and particularly in the province of Quebec. First-as mentioned in the reports of the Canadian Economic Council-there is of course the scarcity of money; the increase in the lot prices due to speculation; the famous 11 per cent tax on building materials which the government insists on maintaining; and also the failure of the federal authorities to show leadership.
Of course, economic factors are involved. If this government had kept its promise when it came to power two years ago, and if it had ensured that so widely heralded prosperity, I think that today many more workers would have the means to buy a house. Under the circumstances, I think that it is our duty to suggest corrective measures or at least solutions.
Before making suggestions to the minister, inasmuch as he asked for our assistance in this field, I should like him to tell me whether he is really sincere and responsible when he says that he wants to take all the necessary measures to rectify the present tragic housing situation. Can the minister give us his assurance that he will contribute to the settlement of that problem? Is he ready to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials? He would show good will, a really deep feeling for the people who elected this government and he would also recognize a need. I should like the minister to tell us whether he is prepared to go that far.
I should like him also to tell us why the government has left the interests accumulate to the point where the lending rate is almost prohibitive. I do not know of any family head earning an average salary of $6,000 or $7,000 a year who can buy a house, make his monthly payments, pay the interest, pay back the principal, pay the municipal and school taxes, the local improvement taxes and also maintain his property. The minister knows full well that it is not realistic to ask a head of a large family or a man with only a few children to make ends meet with the continued increase in the cost of living, which this government is unable to curb.
Does the minister really believe that the policies which he is now elaborating are of such nature as to improve the situation? I do not think so, because it is humanly and materially unrealistic.
The attitude of the present government is so different from the election promises made by our friends opposite in 1965 that I would

speechtext:
Yes, I look it and I am not
ashamed of it like some Tories apparently appear to be. I don't give a damn for the $25,000 per year supporter of the Tory party, nor whether he can find a house as long as I can find adequate housing for the lunch pail carriers in my riding. They are my concern.
Don't run away with yourself, Bryce.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member should be careful of his public image to which we have been exposed for years. That image is likely to go out the window if an intellectual such as he decides to interrupt and interfere from his seat. You have a public image now, and you have a responsibility.
Don't worry, our boys are not particularly concerned about-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Don't let your image go to your head. Please be calm. Don't get excited. You should co-operate or co-ordinate your housing committee a little better.
Now that we have got over that little bit of interruption, let me refer to last Saturday's edition of the Montreal Star. I sat thinking that if I were a young executive in Montreal and wanted to find a house to live in, would I have any success. As has been mentioned here today, many young couples are starting out in life and want to obtain a little bungalow on a piece of land 50 feet by 100 feet. I was wondering where I could find such a property in that big, bustling metropolis of Montreal.
In looking at the Montreal Star I first found an ad for a five and one half room bungalow at $13,530 in Chateauguay, which is a village 15 minutes from Dorchester street, with payments of $82 a month. Another firm advertised three and four bedroom bungalows for $15,399. The ad suggested that one should hurry because there were only 1,000 left. If one preferred a duplex in St. Laurent at $39,000, which means about $19,000 per unit, a few of those can be found right in the heart of old French Canada.
In the event that some individuals on the other side are contemplating a move to la belle province during this 100th year of confederation, when so many individuals are endorsing federalism, let me refer them to this ad. It refers to a house called the Californian which sells for $18,000 with a 6| per cent interest rate and a cash down payment of $990. Finally, Mr. Chairman, before someone over there has a heart attack because I am not moving along fast enough, there is another house advertised here.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
This next example shows just how important Ross Thatcher is. You can buy a house called "Saskatchewan" for $13,990, with a down payment of $475. Just in case hon. members think that in the question of housing we are forgetting the Quebec nationalists, we find a house called "Quebec" that sells at $16,150 with a tremendous down payment of $800. We have other models ranging from $13,000 to $18,000.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Yes, because I like to hear a good fellow.
September 28, 1967
My question is simply this. I should like to ask the hon. member how long he thinks he would have to spend in the reading room to find ads for the 250,000 houses that he is describing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Is the hon. member asking whether there are 250,000 such homes available?
I believe there is a demand for and a shortage of houses to that extent at least.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was so impressed by the arguments advanced today by the opposition, which arguments were so well documented, that there were absolutely no homes available in this category in the great metropolitan area of Montreal that I went to find out for myself what the figures were.
There is no crisis?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The hon. member is getting
like the hon. member for Kamloops, who has left the chamber to get a tranquillizer. However, Mr. Chairman, there is a serious note to this debate. Perhaps my happy mood tonight will counterbalance the debate we have heard from the other side of the chamber. Hon. members opposite have been extremely critical of our housing policy, but they should be more factual in their remarks. I suppose the new look over there has unfortunately not had time to develop. One would think that the chairman of their committee would have pointed out the excellent work carried out by C.M.H.C. We should have heard of the advantages of having this great corporation rather than the completely misinformed statements to which we have been subjected today.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi said that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour will again rise and hide behind the constitution. I have not had the experience of the hon. member in being a demagogue. I have not had the chance to go across the country and take my own, unofficial poll on the sex life of the tsetse fly or what the big problem is in Vancouver or Winnipeg. I have not had the advantage of the weekly bulletins that have been issued when the hon. member has discovered that Vancouver is worried about pollution, Saskatchewan is worried about external affairs, and deep in the heart of Montreal somebody is worried about separatism.
Supply-Labour
You sound like an auctioneer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am worried about the constitution, and unlike the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, I respect it. There is a fundamental difference here. All of us who have sat in this House of Commons have heard innumerable speeches by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi in which he has defended the right of the province of Quebec and other provinces, and castigated the government for injecting themselves into the affairs of the provinces and now disregards those rights.
What about housing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: All right.

We haven't seen the
hon. member for Yukon for one year.
But when I speak, I contribute something to the debate, unlike the hon. member who has just interjected.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want the attitude of the committee to become belligerent. In all fairness to the hon. member for Yukon, I would point out that he is a perfect example of how we should conduct ourselves in this House of Commons. So I am on his side; other hon. members should leave him alone.
Let us talk about housing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Somebody said that the province of Quebec is finally establishing a housing corporation. I think the hon. member for Sainte-Marie pointed out that in the years 1960 to 1966 the Lesage government would not do any such thing and now, after the enlightened separatist government came into power in the province of Quebec, they will get every nickel possible out of the federal government by having funds funnelled into the province. In the Tory years you had no housing problem because the people stayed in the country and on the farms. They were not inclined to leave the farms, realizing the degree of depression that existed in the big cities. That is the big difference between those days and today.
The minister told the house this afternoon that eight of the provinces have now established what might be called housing authorities or housing corporations. At least they are provincial government bodies working largely in complete co-operation with the federal government.

September 28, 1967
Supply-Labour
The minister in charge of housing in Quebec, Hon. Paul Dozois, is a capable and excellent man. He realizes the necessity for low rental housing in the province of Quebec. He realized this necessity back in the 1950's, and there is in that province what is known as the Dozois plan, or Dozois development, which provides adequate housing for hundreds and hundreds of families in the low rental categories. He is a strong Canadian and a strong federalist. I point this out because I may have created the impression that all members of that government are Noel Tremblays.
But not one single housing corporation at the provincial level was established prior to 1964. Where was this great degree of co-operation between the years 1958 and 1962? Where was the respect for the rights of the provinces in those years? Why did not the great Tory provinces get around to forming housing corporations in those years? They did not do this until there was in Ottawa an enlightened Liberal government.
The facts are there for all to see. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre likes his facts to be precise. He is looking at me now with both eyes, for a change. The Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation was established in 1966. The Nova Scotia Housing Commission was established on April 6, 1966. The New Brunswick Housing Corporation was established on July 1, 1967. The Quebec Housing Corporation, Societe d'habi-tation du Quebec, was assented to on June 29, 1967, and became operative on September 27, 1967. The Ontario Housing Corporation was established on May 8, 1964. The Manitoba Housing and Renewal Corporation was established on June 21, 1967. The Alberta Housing and Urban Renewal Corporation was established on April 11, 1967. The Prince Edward Island Housing Authority was established on April 7, 1966.
Despite these facts, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi rises in the house and accuses the minister of running back and forth across the country holding meetings with the provinces, with nothing to show for his efforts. All the minister has to show for his efforts is six or seven new housing corporations.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
These housing corporations and authorities have been established because we have enlightened legislation. Because of the policy of this government we will be able to do something to solve this problem. We

will be able to provide low rental housing and housing renewals. Not one person in the opposition congratulated the minister today for not having increased the interest rate on loans for low-rental houses. Not one member of the opposition has noticed that the money available for low rental housing in this country is still at an interest rate of 6J per cent. Why did not somebody mention that fact?
If we want to respect the British North America Act in this country, if we want a country-this is the point-everybody must make a sacrifice, and this includes the English separatists as well as the French separatists. If we are to respect the B.N.A. Act and provincial jurisdiction in the field of housing, the name of the game is co-operation. Three levels of government merged to produce Expo, and three levels of government will merge to solve the housing problem. The three levels of government are going to merge right across this country to wipe out slums and eradicate mediocre housing. This can be achieved if we take advantage of the legislation, not that we will adopt but which already exists.
There is not a member in this House of Commons who does not feel as I do in this respect. Sometimes you get a call on Friday night or on Saturday, or a phone call from a constituent who wants to find a senior-citizens home and says, "Is there a home somewhere to place my parents? My mother and father want to live with us, but my home is too small and we do not have anywhere to put them." There is no way in which I can answer this question. We do not have a single, solitary housing development for senior citizens in a city of 90,000 people. This is a shame but it is not the fault of the federal government. There has been sufficient money but, as the minister pointed out time and time again and as has been stated by previous speakers, there has not been one single solitary project brought before the federal government-and I presume the same has been true of the opposition when it formed the government-by the provinces that has ever been refused. The moneys available for low rental housing on the federal level have never been exhausted in one calendar year.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
So let us remember and let us be factual. There is a housing problem and I am not proud of it. This government, like all other governments, must do something about it. However, this is a worldwide problem. I have often been accused of a slight leftist tendency which makes me look from time to time to
September 28, 1967

the little group in the corner and wonder why they are so misguided in other areas. So I went to the library and I said to myself: perhaps we can learn from Sweden. This socialistic haven may have been able to solve this problem. It is a small and compact country. Its people are used to regimentation, they are used to socialism. They do not really have to use the thought process. There cannot be a housing problem in Sweden, I thought. However, I found to my surprise that the waiting list for houses is getting shorter; you only have to wait between five and six years for a house. That is an improvement when you compare it with Poland, for instance.
The problem is a worldwide one but it does not mean that we do not have a responsibility to do something about housing. What we have to do is to establish priorities and find out who is important and who needs the housing. Many speakers on the other side of the house have said-and unfortunately their remarks got lost in their partisan attitude- that we must do something for the little man with the lunch pail. It is hard to shed tears for the young executive making $28,000 a year who cannot find a mortgage at 6.25 per cent. I stay away from the executive page in the Montreal Star, the $40,000 and up category. There are many of them. But we need low rental housing.
Let us eliminate the term "public housing". It is degrading, to my way of thinking. Not being an intellectual, an engineer or an architect, I can never understand why public housing has to be so ugly, why it cannot be more functional and why we cannot have a little grass growing around it. Why is it that a man who earns $100 or $120 a week is not entitled to decent housing? The provision of decent housing is the moral obligation of the government and we have no right to shift it to the provinces or the municipalities. We are not trying to do so. We are trying to co-operate, and this is the reason why the minister, particularly in the first three months of the year, travelled from one end of the country to the other setting up housing corporations. So the mechanism and good will are there, but the demand for this type of housing must be generated by the people on the street, the people at the civic level who have a moral responsibility through the church and social groups to look after their neighbour. It is a grave responsibility, and yet when one goes to city council meetings, as I do-and I am sure this is true all across the country-one finds only eight or nine people present there. One can understand then the despair and
Supply-Labour
frustrations of the old people because they cannot find homes since there are not enough convalescent and low rental homes available. These places do not have to be shacks. Let us look at Habitat which we are proud to show the world. We are trying to do things in this country but we will not get anywhere if the attitude of the opposition is completely negative and partisan. We have not heard a single, solitary suggestion from the other side except for the one made by the hon. member for Northumberland who said we should use moral persuasion on insurance companies. That is his great idea for the future. Other proposals came from the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi who filed eight or nine suggestions that are two or three years old and already on the statute books.
I just received a note from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation stating that their pamphlet is out of date. However, that is not too important because the principle is the same, namely that there is money and there always has been money for low rental housing. What we want to do is rid the country of the prejudice that surrounds the name of public housing. We want to cease equating public housing with poverty, degradation and second class status. We want to make our low rental housing projects in this country attractive and a compliment to the working man. It is not the 8.25 per cent interest that is the burden in housing, as the hon. member for Sainte-Marie said in one of his few moments of rationality. It is the taxes on the municipal level for schools that fall on the home owner. The day is rapidly waning for the hope that all of us have of living on a piece of land 50 by 100 feet with a nice little cottage on it and a few tomato plants growing in the backyard. It is impossible. There are no more lots left on Dorchester street or Sherbrooke street in Montreal. If you want that dream, you have to go back to the country and when you get back to the country you are faced with the tremendous cost of building facilities for education. It is a vicious circle. It is not a problem that one level of government can settle. It is a problem which has become a national emergency. I do not know if the minister will agree with that. Nevertheless, in times of national emergency we should not fight, bicker, and pass the buck. The time has come for complete cooperation among the civic, provincial and federal jurisdictions. Fortunately, through the foresight, intelligence, integrity and eloquence of the minister, practically every

September 28, 1967
Business of the House province in Canada today has finally established a provincial housing corporation the medium through which we will eradicate the slums of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I see that I do not have much time left and I think I should congratulate the hon. member for Verdun for that non-partisan speech which he promised us and delivered to us. Perhaps he will excuse me for being slightly partisan in the minute or so that is left to us today. However, I have no intention of blasting the minister. I think that, along with many members on this side of the house I can say we have a great deal of regard for him and for his capabilities. However, we must realize that he is an overworked man. It is not his fault that he was saddled with this responsibility for housing. We know that within the terms of reference of his portfolio there is plenty of work for any man even though his capacity may be great to carry out his duties in that respect. Nevertheless, the housing policy has suffered, I think. I do not believe we can blame the minister for that.
I was very interested tonight to hear the hon. member for Middlesex East mention the resolution that was passed by the council of the city of London. It is recognized at the present time in the city of London that there is a shortage there of some 4,000 dwelling units. They are quite concerned, and I am sure everybody in the house is concerned about the fact that throughout Canada there is a shortage of some 25,000 residential units.
This is what we are considering here now. I hope we will have an opportunity to carry on this discussion a little further some time in the not too distant future and to discuss this problem in greater detail. I am concerned about the effect of the increase in the maximum interest rate upon the average person who makes less than $8,000 a year, not the man who is fortunate enough to be in the higher income bracket. What will happen to him, because with the higher interest rate naturally the valuation of all homes will increase the inflationary pressures which exist today? When it does, the man living in the low rental home will have to pay more by way of rent. Naturally, the money coming out of his pocket will remove him from that utopian condition of having his own home.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Is the home, the private dwelling, becoming uneconomic? I do not think so. The minister ought to consider that. Particularly, he ought to consider the fellow in the lower income

bracket. How is he to have a home of his own?
I note some restlessness, Mr. Chairman. May I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

September 28. 1967	COMMONS
It is a known fact that the Estates General will bring together 2,500 delegates who will study in committee the problems of Quebecers and Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ESTATES GENERAL OF QUEBEC AND FRENCH CANADA
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member tells us that last June-

maintopic: ESTATES GENERAL OF QUEBEC AND FRENCH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister will certainly have the opportunity to reply; in fact, he will have three minutes to reply.
So, I consider strange this refusal of the government or of the Liberal party or of the federal Liberal members from Quebec, except the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who has agreed to attend the meetings of the Estates General, the object of which is precisely to consider the problems of the Quebecers.
It is known that at their meeting in Montmorency House, the federal Liberal members were told by Reverend Father Ares, a Jesuit well known for his concern for national questions, that they have been too aloof from the main events that have occurred in Quebec recently.
And they still do since, generally speaking, the federal members of parliament refuse to take part in as important a meeting as that of the Estates General to be held next November.
It is therefore astonishing to hear the hon. Minister of Justice tell us, as if he no longer knows what is going on in Quebec and how the thinking evolves: If they have suggestions to make and amendments to propose to the constitution, let them do so. But he does not have any to make, precisely because he shies away from the events and the changing mood in Quebec. He stays far from it and does not participate in the life of present day Quebec; that is why he has no suggestions to make. He has no plans to amend the constitution, and merely says: If anyone has suggestions to make, let him make them.

But when one makes suggestions-and that is what is going on right now, in the case of all the suggestions made to the hon. Minister of Justice-the hon. minister merely rejects them and does not make any of his own.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that if the hon. Minister of Justice, whose mission, whose role is precisely to attend to constitutional changes when they are indicated, were to follow more closely what goes on in Quebec at the present time, if he met Quebecers oftener, he would know what amendments are indicated.
Perhaps it is because he was elected in an English-speaking riding in Montreal that he seems to neglect the point of view of the French Canadians. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. Minister of Justice, as a man in public life and a Quebecer of French extraction, should take part in the Estates General. He should attend the meetings, participate in the discussions and hear the various points of view which will be expressed. What will be the conclusions thereof? I do not know, since the Estates General have not yet met, but I think it would be profitable for the Minister of Justice to hear and discuss all those suggestions at the Estates General. I also think that it would be more useful for him than to argue that Estates General are a backward step and only those who are elected can speak on behalf of the people.
No, Mr. Speaker, it does not only rest with those who have been elected to speak on behalf of Quebec citizens; it rests with the Quebecers themselves to speak on their own behalf. It rests with the Quebecers to speak for themselves and this is what they are going to do at that meeting of the Estates General which includes delegates of every constituency, of all classes of society and of every association.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In concluding, I invite the minister to change his mind and to allow the Estates General to have access to all documents, statistics and research which might have been made by the federal government in the past. By making all those available to the Estates General, I think that it will give the best opportunity to study the Quebec problem, since this has been organized quite seriously by a group of honest men who really want to study the Quebec problem fully.
The Estates General will elect, as I said earlier, people from all walks of life and every part of Quebec. The organization was

That is why I invite him to change his mind in that respect, to recognize the wonderful work accomplished by the Estates General up to date, to take part in it, to voice his opinion and to make available to that organization all the research and statistics facilities of the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ESTATES GENERAL OF QUEBEC AND FRENCH CANADA
speechtext:
My Speaker, my point of order dealt with the allegation of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) to the effect that his question of last June concerned the participation of the Liberal party in the Estates General, whereas it referred to something entirely different. As a matter of fact, it was about statistics to be supplied by the federal government to that organization.
I feel, therefore, that he is clearly misusing the standing orders so as to deal with anything and everything when it suits his convenience. That is why I have no advice to take from the hon. member for Lapointe who is lacking in sense of sequence.
He is also anything tout well-read and has a very bad memory. He says that I failed to make any suggestions to amend the constitution. I must tell him that hardly three weeks ago, at the convention of the Canadian Bar Association held in Quebec city, I made very specific suggestions to amend the constitution, to ensure its gradual rather than disorderly evolution and development.
These propositions, Mr. Speaker, are the only definite propositions made by a government in power in this country to amend the constitution.
So, there are people who have been making haphazard and contradictory propositions, for a very long term but, our government excepted, no one has yet suggested a definite formula for the orderly and progressive development of the constitution.
As far as the Estates General are concerned, in Le Devoir, day before yesterday, in a paper read to the delegates who are to sit on the Estates General, I see that the right and the duty of French Canadians to be equal to other people is being proclaimed.
Mr. Speaker, in my speech to the Bar Association, I suggested a way through which French-speaking Canadians could obtain equal rights with English-speaking Canadians. This suggestion has been rejected and even ignored by the hon. member.

speechtext:
Even by the right hon.
Prime Minister.
