maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-WASKESIU, SASK.-POSSIBLE RETENTION OF TOURIST CABINS

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-WASKESIU, SASK.-POSSIBLE RETENTION OF TOURIST CABINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) is not in the house tonight as I should like to discuss a matter which comes under his jurisdiction. However, I shall take this opportunity to present my case for the Waskesiu townsite national park in Saskatchewan. I would be failing in my duty as a member of parliament, whose constituents are involved in this matter, if I did not do so.
Waskesiu was dedicated by the late prime minister of Canada, W. L. Mackenzie King, as a park for the use of the average Canadian. It was never intended as a rich man's paradise. The original intention of Mr. King with regard to this park has been carried out in that it has largely been used by Canadians of modest means. They have made use of the magnificent setting of Prince Albert national park to erect tents, portable cabins and what are popularly known as shack tents.
Shack tents in reality are collapsible, are readily stored, have wooden walls and a canvas roof. Many of these cabins or shack tents have been passed from father to son and so on. They have been improved and decorated, and in many instances become difficult to recognize in that the improvements have been so vast that the original canvas roofed shack tent is no more. Instead, you might see a gleaming example of what modern technology can do.
The important thing is that Waskesiu provided many thousands of citizens with an opportunity to have an exciting outdoor
September 28, 1967	COMMONS DEBATES	2641
holiday at minimum cost. The portable cabin and shack tent dwellers have been the backbone, the mainstay, of Waskesiu, and in view of this you can imagine the shock and disbelief of Waskesiu enthusiasts at the announcement of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
In place of the camping area, the shack tents, the portable cabins, even the commercial Waskesiu bungalow cabins, a new recreation area and a new group of so called low cost motels is to rise. As a result of the grandiose plans of the minister the tennis courts, bowling greens and other excellent recreational facilities will disappear. In other words, no longer are the needs of those who have made Waskesiu the holiday home it is today to be considered by the minister.
By some strange survey the minister has decided that the one day visitor, the one day transient, is the one his department should woo. This is the decision, even in the face of the fact that the gates of Prince Albert National Park are between 250 to 300 miles from the trans-Canada highway. So, by his decision, the minister is ignoring completely the rights of the present users of Waskesiu. No longer, with the implementation of this plan, will a shack tent owner be able to pass the ownership on to his son; no longer will it be possible for a portable cabin to be passed on to a beneficiary or sold.
In many cases the owners will be faced with losses amounting to $5,000, $6,000 or $7,000, and all of this is to satisfy the whims of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. What is the purpose behind this scheme? Surely it is clear that the purpose is to banish the shack tent, the portable cabin and, later, larger cottage owners, because it is noted that no provision is made for relocation of the shack tents or cabins. It has been said that there is no place to put them. Yet, only 30 acres are involved out of over 30,000 acres which are available in the park in the Waskesiu town site. Lake Waskesiu alone has many areas where cabins could be relocated or, alternatively, where the day camp proposals of the minister could be put to the test.
Make no mistake; if you remove and banish the people who are the backbone of Waskesiu, you destroy the true purpose for which Prime Minister Mackenzie King inaugurated the Prince Albert National Park. The minister should reconsider the plans which were so hastily conceived. Surely, it could not have been his intention to hurt first of all those shack tent owners who can least
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion afford a change. Without Waskesiu many will be unable to afford any summer holiday. I find it difficult to believe that the minister will press forward with such a policy without the benefit of sober second thought. I bring this to the attention of the minister, and I ask him and his officials to consider this issue which is very serious indeed in the province of Saskatchewan.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-WASKESIU, SASK.-POSSIBLE RETENTION OF TOURIST CABINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
should like to assure the hon. member opposite that his remarks this evening were timely and I will draw them to the attention of the minister on his return to the house. There are, however, a couple of points I should like to make today in view of the hon. member's remarks.
Our national parks have been established for the preservation of Canada's marvellous wilderness as our national heritage. It is the desire of the government of Canada to make the parks freely available for the use of all Canadian citizens. The increase in the number of good highways in the last few years has made a large number of Canadians more aware of the national parks and has given them an increasing desire to visit them. Due to this increase in attendance in the national parks, existing facilities definitely have become overcrowded. Therefore, new facilities must be created for the highly mobile type of park visitor that is the norm in this country today. The position of the shack tent dwellers in Waskesiu is a highly privileged one in that they have been allowed to maintain what is, in effect, a private dwelling for some years.
I should at this time emphasize that no existing shack tent dweller in the park today will be displaced. They will continue to be granted leases on a year to year basis so long as the existing tenant or his or her spouse wish to remain there. What the department has said, however, is that no new people will be allowed to obtain leases of this type in the parks. Shack tent camping is a privilege that will rest with the individual and cannot be considered an interest vested in either the structure or the land. A tenant, therefore, cannot be allowed to assign or transfer his lease to somebody other than his or her spouse.
Mr. Speaker, this is a decision that has been discussed at great length in parliament, in our committee and in the press; it is believed to be the right one. Both the minister

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and I firmly believe that a national park is the property of all Canadians and should be available to visitors from all parts of the country. We have gone to great pains to assure those people now holding special shack tent privileges in the park that they will be allowed to remain there as long as they renew their leases annually.
The formation of new private dwellings of this nature, however, would be incompatible with the philosophy of the use of the national park and the increasing need for camp site space for the mobile traveller. It is for this reason that the government believes, in the interests of the public of Canada, that the shack tents must be phased out by natural attrition over the years.
May I say, in conclusion, that the government at all times welcomes the advice of the public and is willing to receive representations from all interested parties including the hon. member.

maintopic: POWER-COLUMBIA RIVER-ALLEGED DELAY IN FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO B.C.
POWER-COLUMBIA RIVER-ALLEGED DELAY IN FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 26 I asked the following question as reported in Hansard at page 2482:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the fact that Hon. W. A. C. Bennett, premier of British Columbia, is publicly condemning the government of Canada for failing to pay the $12 million owed to British Columbia for completion of the Duncan Lake dam by July 31 of this year according to the agreement between the federal and provincial governments with respect to the Columbia river treaty, can the minister inform the house of the facts with respect to this intriguing question?
I asked that question because the people of British Columbia are somewhat confused as to what are the facts. I wish to quote briefly from the agreement signed by the government of Canada and British Columbia on July 18, 1963 in relation to the Columbia river treaty. I find the following in clause 15:
Canada and British Columbia will consult as required on technical and other matters of mutual interest with a view to facilitating the implementation of the treaty, avoiding disputes and carrying out this agreement.
What confuses the people of British Columbia is that Mr. Bennett apparently is not taking advantage of that clause in the treaty, but is publicly condemning the federal government. The Vancouver Sun of May 11, 1967 suggests that Mr. Benhett, when asked for his opinion of the treaty, said that the thing at


fault was that the treaty was signed too quickly. He blamed the federal authorities for the arrangement made with the aluminum company for a dam on the Arrow lakes which was three times better than the one provided by the treaty.
The premier of British Columbia officiated recently at the opening of the Duncan lake dam which was completed earlier than anticipated. This is what he had to say according to the Vancouver Sun of Friday, August 18 in its report of this ceremony:
Premier W. A. C. Bennett officially unleashed the water behind Duncan dam-
At the same time, he unleashed his wrath against Ottawa for failing to pay him $12 million in exchange for flood control benefits in the U.S.
Ottawa, he charged, has defaulted on a term of the Columbia River Treaty under which the Duncan dam was built.
And he offered to lend the federal government the money he claimed it owes B.C.
"I offer to lend it to them if they're so hard up," he told reporters immediately before the dam dedication ceremony here.
"Without interest," he added.
Then the newspaper went on to say:
Such was the private wrath of the premier Thursday as he issued his angry charges in stage whispers to reporters attending the event.
He said later:
"This is supposed to be a picnic atmosphere," he told a crowd of about 300 from atop the dam.
"So I won't make any speeches."
The article says later:
"I want to make it clear," he told reporters privately before the luncheon, "that it is not the U.S. who defaulted. It is Ottawa."
He said that, although under the treaty the U.S. is required to pay flood control benefits to the Canadian government, it is Ottawa who is supposed to pay B.C.
He went on to say:
"It's always Ottawa that's to blame," he said.
These are the premier's criticisms of the treaty in the first instance. I have a photograph in my office in which the premier of British Columbia is shown clapping his hands vigorously while the treaty is being signed by the President of the United States at the Peace Arch in British Columbia, on the U.S.-Canada border.
This has created a great deal of confusion in the public mind. In the agreement there is a clause that permits for consultation on these technical and legal matters in order to avoid disputes. Yet the premier of British
September 28, 1967	COMMONS
Columbia is going around the country blaming the federal government in the first instance for signing the treaty anyway, and latterly for failing to pay the $12 million that he claims is owing his province in respect of the early completion of the Duncan dam.
I trust that when the parliamentary secretary replies he will inform the house of the facts, because the people are confused and want to know the truth with respect to this agreement and Premier Bennett's statements.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. B. Siewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: POWER-COLUMBIA RIVER-ALLEGED DELAY IN FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the facts with regard to this situation are as follows. The British Columbia Power and Hydro Authority brought the Duncan dam into operation on July 31, 1967. This dam is the first of three to be completed as part of the Columbia river undertaking.
Article VI (1) C of the Columbia river treaty provides that the United States shall pay to Canada in United States funds the sum of $11,100,000 upon the commencement of operation of the Duncan dam. This payment was not made by the United States to Canada on the date on which it fell due which, as I have indicated, was July 31 of this year. I understand that the authority to
DEBATES	2643
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion make the necessary payment is contained in an appropriations bill which has not been passed by the congress of the United States.
The importance which we attach to receiving this overdue payment at the earliest possible date has been urged on the United States government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) recently spoke in this sense to Mr. Rusk. He also pressed a claim for interest covering the period since the payment fell due on July 31. While the United States authorities may not view the latter in exactly the same light as we do, we believe they share our anxiety to avoid further delay. Moreover, we are now following up our claim for interest in Washington.
The obligation of the government of Canada in this case consists solely in taking all steps necessary to protect Canadian interests by ensuring that the terms of the Columbia river treaty are carried out. This obligation is being fulfilled by this government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been in touch with the premier of British Columbia in order to keep the premier abreast of developments on this matter.
